He says this is how Bridgewater tests a model's diagnosability, but even so it is only an approximation, because the model itself no longer knows what its real reasoning was.

18:24 Bridgewater runs two funds as an AI controlled experiment
Bridgewater runs two production lines internally. One is "human intuition translated into algorithms, with AI assisting", corresponding to Pure Alpha; the other puts AI at the center, where everyone's job is to train the AI, the AI itself makes decisions like whether to buy yen or what will happen to Japanese GDP, and humans only keep gatekeeping on risk control and data acquisition. The human-intuition line is bigger and performs better, but the AI line has only run for two and a half years and is catching up much faster. What Jensen offers is a prediction: in a few more years it will significantly outperform Bridgewater's entire human portfolio. He also says the goal is to close the full investment loop within six to twelve months — wake up in the morning, look at conditions, form a judgment, stress-test it, then decide — and that there will be "harnesses that build harnesses", making it easier and easier to replicate. This is also how he explains why the 6% to 7% productivity growth has not shown up yet: this stuff is hard, you don't just plug it in.

25:33 Don't use China as an excuse not to regulate
To the argument "if we stop, China won't stop", Jensen gives two answers. First, China is moving fast partly because we are moving fast — they are copying what the frontier produces, and we are far ahead on compute and other fronts, so slowing the frontier also slows the copiers. Second, even with zero expectation of cooperation: as long as any model used in the US economy must come from a regulated lab whose goings-on we know, then a Chinese model that wants to operate in the US has to go through the same process, or it doesn't get in. He thinks the more direct instrument is liability rules — if you say you will be liable for the crimes your AI commits, you will naturally slow down; if you can't control it, don't build it. He also mentions that government officials come to him with these questions on their own initiative, their confusion being that they simply don't know where to start, and his answer is to start by understanding.

28:38 Regulating the model isn't enough; you have to regulate the use
Jensen breaks regulation into layers and points out the hard part: regulating the model alone is not enough. The first layer is the lab: the model that committed the crime was unreleased, still in training, so there needs to be a review process like biologics testing, with the power to subpoena employees to testify under oath about how safety is handled and what incidents have occurred. The second layer is the released model and monitoring of its use. The third layer is the most easily overlooked: the same model, given a different harness and a different amount of thinking time, gives different results — the longer it thinks, the better it answers, which is another scaling law — so the people using dangerous models themselves need to clear a safety bar. The fourth layer is open source: once the weights can be downloaded and run locally, there is no central control point, nobody knows what you are asking it, and nobody knows what you are training with it. He says all of this sounds hard, but the option of not doing it is scarier.

32:43 An open model gets stronger when you narrow it
Jensen's analogy: a model's "brain" is a bit like a human brain — the more general, the more useful, but generality sacrifices specialization — Astra is especially good at math because it did a lot of math training. Once you have an open model, you can decide for yourself what it focuses on: accept a general intelligence six to nine months behind the frontier, then use reinforcement learning to train it into an expert at one narrow task, such as reading everything in the world to predict the next earnings report, where it beats humans and stock analysts can no longer compete with it. Two other benefits: what you do stays secret from the labs; and the world doesn't have to let the intelligence of two or three companies rule everything. But he also says unregulated open source is a crazy idea: with weights downloaded locally, nobody knows what you trained it on — people are training bio and hacking models — and within months it will surpass the model that caused the big panic.

44:00 Token spending is up two hundredfold, and it's making money
Bridgewater's token spending is up roughly 200x compared with 2023, and it is making money: its funds charge a fixed fee and a performance fee, and the value AI creates exceeds what they pay for it. Jensen designed it as a flywheel — AI's ability to predict the world earns money, the money goes back into smarter intelligence, smarter intelligence predicts the world better; this is the industry-level moat as he understands it, and also where he judges the shock will come from: companies that can generate revenue and plow it back into intelligence will pull ahead. In his view the bottleneck is no longer model quality but two places: first, human constraints like "scientists and investors collaborating" — investing has no fixed rules, and AI itself is participating in trading, making the past that model training depends on less and less relevant; second, not enough compute and memory, which the whole world is short of.

51:08 We are subsidizing machines replacing human labor
In a New York Times op-ed, Jensen argued for a token tax, that is, a tax on machine labor. The logic: we tax human labor but not machine labor, which is itself giving machine labor a comparative advantage. If a company hires an AI worker, it should at least pay tax at the same rate as the income tax on a human wage, otherwise it is prioritizing machine labor. He thinks the tax is politically viable — Republicans and Democrats can both agree; who would publicly argue that we should incentivize machine labor rather than human labor? He also gives a timeline: within three years, 14% of existing jobs will be completely transformed. He draws an analogy to the populist backlash after China joined the WTO: a new source of labor itself causes a shock, and AI will accelerate it, and if it isn't handled in advance, what gets lost may be more than just AI.

item.title: The Opium War Wasn't Fought for Opium, It Was Fought for Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-youdead-鸦片战争不是为鸦片打的-是为茶叶打的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-youdead-鸦片战争不是为鸦片打的-是为茶叶打的/
item.description: Britain bought Chinese tea but had nothing to sell in return; China took only silver, and the world's silver was drained dry. What Britain finally picked up was Indian opium. The driver of that 1839 war was not opium — it was tea.
item.content:encoded:
Britain bought Chinese tea but had nothing to sell in return; China took only silver, and the world's silver was drained dry. What Britain finally picked up was Indian opium. The driver of that 1839 war was not opium — it was tea.

Yangwen lays out a hard silver–opium–tea chain, and the Industrial Revolution section is counterintuitive too; but the comedy interludes eat up a fair amount of time, so the information density is middling.

8:13 What's in a British tea bag is dust and fannings
Tea is graded by wholeness into four levels: leaf, broken leaf, fannings, dust — the last two being the siftings left over. Yangwen says the British market drinks mainly these two grades, packed into tea bags; China drinks whole leaves, with attention to leaf shape, body, and a complete ritual. Her words were that China doesn't drink dust, only leaves. Hugh jokes that dust sounds like a country singer, and Greg concedes the British really are drinking fannings. Yangwen came to Britain in 1996 and still doesn't understand why milk and sugar go into tea — once added, by her standard it is ‘no longer tea’.

17:26 The Mongols wanted tea, the Central Plains wanted horses
Yangwen says tea defined China's premodern relations with Mongolia and Central Asia. Nomadic peoples didn't settle, and needed tea, iron pots, and silk, which could only be obtained from China; China was a rice-and-wheat farming civilisation and lacked horses. Hence the historical tea-horse exchange, trading goods at fixed ratios. Once the relationship broke down, the Mongols, lacking tea, raided southward — the 1449 Tumu crisis is an example: the Ming army was encircled by the Mongols, and roughly fifty thousand soldiers were captured along with the emperor. Afterward the Ming closed the Great Wall for a time, but blockade was never a long-term solution, and in the end the gates had to reopen for the tea-horse trade.

21:34 The name of tea exposes the routes it travelled
Tea's spread left linguistic traces. Yangwen says that in Mongolian, Russian, Turkish, Arabic, and Persian, tea is called cha, while in English it is tea — the overland camel caravan routes left cha, the sea routes left tea. Greg made up a rhyme for it: ‘If it travels by car, it is cha. If it goes by the sea, it is tea.’ The value of this clue is that the same product entered different civilisations through two completely different trade networks, and even its name forked. Tea reached Europe in the early 17th century, with the Portuguese and the Dutch East India Company as the earliest suppliers.

29:53 China took only silver and drained the world dry
By the late 18th century, China had already sucked the world's silver into its treasury. Yangwen says that from Vasco da Gama's voyage in 1497 to 1793, Europeans and Americans came to buy tea, porcelain, and silk, while China took only gold and silver, and over several centuries the Europeans found they had nothing the Chinese wanted. She quotes the missionary Robert Hart: the Chinese have the best food (rice), the healthiest drink (tea), the best clothing material (silk), and need nothing from Britain. In 1793 the Macartney mission demanded free trade, and the emperor's attitude was: I permit my subjects to sell you a little tea, and that is a favour. The only thing Britain had left that could break into China was Indian opium.

39:04 Stolen green tea grew into black tea in India
In 1843, to break its dependence on Chinese tea, Britain sent the botanist Robert Fortune to infiltrate China's interior and steal tea plants. He bought a fake queue, wore a hat to cover his unshaved forehead, travelled deep into the mountains, and dug up whole tea plants to ship back to Assam in India. Yangwen points out an irony: what he stole was mainly green tea from the southeast coast, and grown in Assam's stronger sunlight and richer soil it turned into black tea — the raw material now regarded as archetypal British black tea is in fact a Chinese green tea variety. Fortune himself did not get rich from it; Yangwen says he was not wealthy when he died.

42:12 The Industrial Revolution was pushed along by tea and sugar
Some economic historians have argued that the Industrial Revolution was driven by tea. Yangwen says caffeine plus the sugar in tea let the working class refuel at half past ten in the morning and half past three in the afternoon, working longer and producing more; Sydney Mintz's Sweetness and Power is the representative statement of this argument. The same logic explains why tea replaced small beer in the mid-18th century as the middle class's breakfast drink of choice. By 1923, 53% of the world's tea supply was being drunk in Britain.

45:13 Britain's tea today comes mainly from Kenya
Tea cultivation followed the colonial map. The seedlings stolen from China first took root in Assam, India, and in 1885 India exported 35,000 tons of tea a year, which Greg converts into 7,000 African elephants. In 1903 Britain opened plantations in Kenya, and Yangwen says Kenya is today Britain's main source of tea. She also notes that Chinese tea bought today at places like Fortnum Mason has mostly been systematically machine-cut, so the leaf shape can't be seen, and what you drink is not the kind of tea she recognises.

48:26 Tea bags cost the British tea's ritual
In the nuance window, Yangwen offers a prediction: tea will revive. The reason is the environmental movement — people should eat natural things and drink natural things, and tea is a plant to begin with, like a vegetable, good for health and the environment; on the other hand, the modernisation of the tea bag makes her feel tea has lost its ritual, and perhaps its nutrition too. Greg steers the topic to the China–Britain difference: in Chinese tea drinking, the waiting itself is the ritual; the British place more emphasis on the time spent chatting with people after the tea is brewed. Hugh admits he has never experienced so-called ‘slow tea’.

item.title: The company that almost built the iPhone died because it didn't believe it had constraints
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cautionary-差点做出-iphone-的公司-死于不认为自己有约束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cautionary-差点做出-iphone-的公司-死于不认为自己有约束/
item.description: General Magic had the biggest industry alliance in history, more money than it could spend, and the best engineers. In six months it sold 3,000 devices. It lacked neither money nor talent — it lacked any belief that it had constraints.
item.content:encoded:
General Magic had the biggest industry alliance in history, more money than it could spend, and the best engineers. In six months it sold 3,000 devices. It lacked neither money nor talent — it lacked any belief that it had constraints.

Tim Harford tells a complete case of "everything was right and it was all wrong," and the two rounds of eliminating explanations for the failure in the back half are worth more than the story itself.

4:28 The iPhone was imagined in 1989
While at Apple's Advanced Technology Group, Peratt used a big red notebook to describe a future information and communication product: it should bring personal satisfaction like jewelry, have perceived value even when unused, offer the comfort of a touchstone, the feel of a shell, the magic of crystal. What he drew was a smooth rectangle, no buttons, only a touchscreen, able to serve as a phone, a messaging device, a portable TV and a game console, and able to book plane tickets. It was 1989; most cell phones were the size of a brick, Apple's new portable computer weighed 16 pounds, and the World Wide Web did not yet exist. He called the idea the pocket crystal, imagining people carrying it everywhere — "if your house caught fire, you'd think, first save the family, then grab my pocket crystal." He told Bill Atkinson, and Atkinson brought in Andy Hertzfeld, two of the core programmers of the original Macintosh.

9:40 A company with no product can still make Wall Street line up
General Magic had no profits, no revenue, not even a product — only an idea — and it issued stock to ordinary retail investors. Goldman Sachs bankers shoved each other to grab allocations; one banker asked, "What's it going to take? Would taking off my shirt be enough?" and then actually did it, standing half-naked in the conference room. The stock doubled immediately after listing. Every partner in the alliance had already put in millions of dollars each. As one vice president in the book told David Epstein, they had so much money they never had to worry about making payroll — what startup never has to worry about making payroll? That is the key mechanism: enough money that no one ever has to make a trade-off.

12:46 The tech was so good it made a partner's department obsolete on the spot
Two young engineers flew to Japan to show a hardware prototype to Mitsubishi. The demo had barely started when the host suddenly called in a group of employees in work clothes, apologized, and asked them to run it from the beginning — because this thing had no modem, it was all implemented in software. A groan came from the audience, and a manager named Kato slumped forward and put his head on the table. The host apologized again: "You just made Kato's department obsolete." This technology made answering machines, arcades, books, keyboards and mice obsolete. At the same time they built the precursor to USB cables, a new programming language called Telescript, called portable networking the cloud, put skeuomorphic icons on a touchscreen, and built a store where you could buy applications — back when no one called it an app store.

17:55 They built the future but not a product
The first device running the General Magic operating system was Sony's Magic Link in 1994. Behind the gorgeous graphics it was hard to use, shipping with a 200-page manual; it was the size of a hardcover book, its grayscale monochrome touchscreen only the size of a postcard, and it ran on old-fashioned AA batteries that drained extremely fast. No Wi-Fi and no Bluetooth; the body had only an old-style telephone jack — sending messages and making calls both meant sitting at a desk plugged into a phone line, and it didn't even have a built-in cell phone. In today's purchasing power, about $1,600. Sony sold 3,000 units in the first six months, mostly to friends and family of General Magic employees. A few years later, Apple sold about 300,000 iPhones on day one. Motorola's Envoy in 1995 had wireless communication, but cost nearly twice as much as the Magic Link.

20:00 eBay's idea was called the dumbest thing a colleague had ever heard
Pierre, a technical support engineer at General Magic, built a webpage on the side: put your unused stuff at home up there and let others bid. He named the site AuctionWeb, showed it to colleagues, and asked whether he could spin it out as a company, or whether General Magic would invest. One colleague's response was typical: this is the dumbest idea I've ever heard — you want strangers to trust each other on the internet? Good luck, we're not interested. This quiet man was Pierre Omidyar, and that website was eBay, which later made him a billionaire. It is also the epitome of General Magic missing the Web — people inside reminded management daily, and management always found a reason to ignore it.

24:06 Missing the Web was embarrassing, but not the cause of death
In the documentary, former employees talk about missing the World Wide Web with laughter and sighs mixed together, but Tim Harford argues this failure is a distraction. When the Magic Link launched in 1994, the Web was still a curiosity; even if it had been Web-compatible, that wouldn't have been enough to make people pay the equivalent of $3,000 for a Motorola Envoy. The second explanation is "too early": by the time the iPhone launched in 2007, memory prices had fallen 1,000-fold from 1994, a typical microprocessor had 500 times the computing power, and there was Wi-Fi, 3G and a Web with real content. That technology gap is real, but one tech commentator in the documentary says General Magic could never have succeeded no matter what it did, and Tim says: that sounds plausible, but he's wrong.

29:19 They had time to write the calendar back to the start of astronomical time
Epstein's argument is that General Magic had no constraints at all: the best hardware and software engineers, excellent design and marketing, a charismatic prophet-like leader, plus Apple's investment, millions from each alliance partner, and retail investors' money. With both talent and time, why compromise — just go build the pocket crystal, even if early-1990s technology simply couldn't build it. The consequence was that no one was forced to think clearly about what they were actually doing: when they described their target market they said Joe Sixpack, meaning everyone. So the product got stuffed with an instrument panel, a big emoji of a walking lemon, a coin-flip animation. The coin flip came from co-founder Andy Hertzfeld, a man who at the time clearly felt he had all the time in the world. The calendar originally covered only 1904 to 2096, a few lines of code, but it was first changed to the year 1 AD, then to the beginning of astronomical time.

33:33 Tony Fadell asked only two questions
Tony Fadell used to call every day begging General Magic for a job, and when the company collapsed he was heartbroken, but he learned something. At his next company, he focused on just two things: given today's technology, what is new, exciting and possible? The answer was MP3s and ever-cheaper hard drives, and combining the two could make a digital music player that made Walkmans and CD players obsolete. The second question was what deadline to set for himself. The answer: it's January 2001, we ship before Christmas. The company he joined was Apple, and what shipped on time a few weeks before Christmas was the iPod — doing one thing beautifully. That restraint paved the way for the next project, the pocket crystal that was actually built: the iPhone. His colleague Andy Rubin later founded Android, and others co-founded LinkedIn, ran Google Search, and led Apple's AI, Safari and Apple Watch.

item.title: Numerical Control Didn't De-skill Machinists; Average Skill Barely Moved
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-asianometry-数控机床没让技工降级-平均技能水平几乎没变/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-asianometry-数控机床没让技工降级-平均技能水平几乎没变/
item.description: Since the 1950s, people have feared that numerical control would de-skill machinists. But the hourly wages of A-grade machinists and NC operators were nearly identical, and over three decades overall skill fell only about 1%.
item.content:encoded:
Since the 1950s, people have feared that numerical control would de-skill machinists. But the hourly wages of A-grade machinists and NC operators were nearly identical, and over three decades overall skill fell only about 1%.

Worth hearing for anyone concerned with how automation rewrites skills and wages: this episode uses three data sets — training time, headcount, and wages — to test a widely believed claim.

1:04 A machinist's job isn't just cutting metal
A machinist doesn't just operate a machine tool to cut metal. They work with designers to read two-dimensional drawings, reconstruct them in their head as three-dimensional parts, and spot what can't be made ahead of time, which calls on geometry, trigonometry, and algebra. What's truly hard to replace is feel: the 1887 book The Complete Practical Machinist says lathe work is most particular about feed and speed, the most varied, complex, and deceptive part of the whole trade, requiring judgment, perception, and alertness — the tool may sound and look fine while actually drifting off, even producing scrap or injuring someone. An experienced person, using gauges plus feel, can detect dimensional changes as small as one half thousandths of an inch. Skill here equals judgment, and this is the bullseye of the later de-skilling debate.

3:06 Four years and eight thousand hours to become a journeyman
In the first half of the twentieth century, machining was the largest single skilled manufacturing job for American men, and the standard entry path was a formal apprenticeship: generally four years, eight thousand hours; tool and die makers five years, ten thousand hours. Someone who apprenticed at GE in the 1940s recalled spending the first half year learning basics in the shop, with classes three evenings a week in shop math, college physics, reading drawings, and electricity; then three and a half years rotating through various tools, starting at the drill press, changing about every half year. On completion the company certified you as a journeyman, issued your first set of tools or a cash bonus, and raised your pay — in his words, you were finally qualified for marriage. But this was never the only path: there were those who came up purely through shop experience and self-study at home, and there were courses claiming to teach you how to operate a machining shop, which you could call the 1930s coding bootcamp.

6:10 Riveting a boiler: nine machinists become one
Industrialization repeatedly does the same thing: pack skill into the machine, then break the work into pieces. When Edison started making light bulbs in 1880, the factory was full of skilled craftsmen who understood glass and wire and knew from scratch how to make a bulb; as specialized machines built their skills in, the work was simplified and segmented, and a few all-around craftsmen were replaced by a large group of workers each knowing one operation. Riveting a boiler originally took nine skilled machinists; with a hydraulic riveter it became one skilled worker plus eight unskilled ones, the latter doing things like clamping. In 1883 the young machinist John Morrison testified before Congress that the machining trade had been subdivided since the mid-1870s, and subdivided again after that, so that in making sewing machines, for example, the jobs were split so finely that a person hardly counted as a machinist. NC is just one more step on this timeline.

8:14 Bosses hoping NC would save labor were disappointed first
NC controls the machine tool and workpiece with pre-programmed instructions, without requiring a machinist's direct manual intervention: a programmer translates the drawing into coordinates, punches them onto paper or plastic tape, and feeds them into the controller. It was invented in the 1950s, but at first served only the Air Force and aerospace, with specifications far beyond the needs of ordinary shops and small workshops. Crucially, early NC was hardwired, with limited functions, and a major change meant tearing apart the controller and rebuilding it, very inflexible. So shop owners hoping to use it to lower worker skill were thoroughly disappointed: a mid-1960s survey by Lawrence Williams and Brian Williams found shops still needed operators with the same skills and technical knowledge, especially right after introduction; owners felt the risk of NC breaking down and causing expensive downtime was too high, and instead assigned their best employees to run the machine. Once it matured, the advantages showed — one NC drill press was estimated to equal three conventional machines.

11:19 Training shrank from five years to half a year
In the 1970s computer technology accelerated NC's spread, and by 1980, 25% to 30% of machine tools sold in developed economies had NC. The real de-skilling evidence came from training time and headcount: a 1982 paper studying Swedish machining shops noted that NC operators needed at most 6 to 12 months of training, while lathe operators had to grind through 4 to 5 years in the shop. In cases cited by the paper, one plant needed only 22 NC operators instead of 44 lathe operators; another replaced 63 qualified machine operators with 21 NC operators. In a developed country like Sweden, skilled workers willing to work night shifts were hard to find, and NC operators could accept stranger hours, so the machines didn't have to stop. As for whether this was lower skill, in a 1980s survey of Canadian hand machinists nearly 80% agreed NC required fewer skills, yet only half of those who had actually operated NC saw it that way.

15:21 NC operators' hourly wage differed by only twenty-one cents
Wages are a crude ruler for skill, but the result is counterintuitive. A 1989 study using 1981 U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data compared the average wages of 80,000 A-grade machinists and NC operators in the machine tool industry: A-grade machinists earned $9.72 an hour, NC operators $9.51. For comparison, A-grade machinists still earned more than B- and C-grade machinists doing more repetitive work ($8.54 and $6.41); interestingly, there is evidence that some NC operators were recruited from B- and C-grade machinists, meaning they were actually the ones getting a raise. Of course wages are affected by region, unions, and so on, and don't reflect job quality or the number of positions. Bill Bowman is the other side: as more and more people learned the skills he had, his CNC premium was flattened, and a few years later, combined with layoffs, he was making only $20,000 a year.

18:25 Over thirty years overall skill fell only about 1%
Jeffrey Keefe's 1991 study examined three U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics surveys spanning 30 years and found overall skill levels fell by about 1% — essentially zero. This number directly refutes the claim that numerical control de-skilled machinists. But the author also stresses that the unchanged average masks changes in job composition: the work of skilled setup workers, semi-skilled machine operators, and unskilled workers changed or disappeared, and other tasks migrated to NC operators, so underneath it was very turbulent. So the more accurate statement is not that skills disappeared, but that the form of skill changed — deep mastery of one thing was weakened and replaced by several other kinds of skill, such as understanding how the whole machine runs and reconstructing the logic of an accident when it fails, which is why operators say you can't just go tear into a fault, you have to work backward to how the accident happened.

19:25 AI coding is replaying this history
What the author sees is a parallel between AI coding and machining back then: early GitHub CoPilot and early Cursor only did simple completion or inserting a line, but now AI coding systems have evolved into agentic — while modern CNC machine tools haven't reached that step. He specifically mentions a February 2026 case study by OpenAI's Ryan Lopopolo about a brand-new product built by a team of agents, with humans monitoring and steering. Programming, like machining back then, is one of America's dominant high-paying jobs; some things don't change — programmers still have to read code and judge where the problem is, only when it's time to fix it you tell the coding agent instead of opening a text editor, the same skills expressed differently. Some jobs will de-skill and decline, new fields may appear, and those are the NC operators of the AI coding era. What he remembers is Bill Bowman: you have to keep learning.

item.title: The case for export controls has retreated all the way down to a single premise that still holds
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cogrev-出口管制的理由一路退守-只剩一个前提说得通/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cogrev-出口管制的理由一路退守-只剩一个前提说得通/
item.description: First it was about military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.
item.content:encoded:
First it was about military use, then it retreated to stopping frontier models, then to limiting how many AI agents China can run; the only self-consistent premise left for this policy is a belief in a short sprint to godlike superintelligence, winner takes all.

A three-hour debrief on a China trip; the second half's analysis of the policy machinery toward China — the drift in the stated rationale for controls, decoupling risk, and alternatives — is more worth hearing than the first half's travelogue.

8:56 What the China discourse lacks is a target state
Nathan says the missing piece in America's discussion of China is a ‘target state’: everyone jumps straight to ‘we have to win’, but nobody answers what winning looks like, what happens if we lose, or whether there is an achievable condition for victory. His proposed goal is Pax Machina, or better, Pax Robotica — the two countries and the world sharing the prosperity and peace of the AI era, robots going into factories, into fields, into homes, while avoiding the AI version of the sword of Damocles. He says explicitly that this is not about winning, it is about arriving together. A competition with no target state leaves nothing but escalation itself.

18:56 China isn't rising, it's returning to historical normal
To the claim that ‘China can't innovate’, Nathan applies one word: cope, and says it is isomorphic to cope in the AI field — conceding that AI has gotten this far while insisting it won't reason, won't discover new knowledge, won't change paradigms. His judgment is that China's return is the long-run historical norm, and that the period he and Dario grew up in — China down, America the sole superpower — was the anomaly. Any effort to slow China's progress can therefore work at most in the short term, and China will be a first-tier player in nearly every major human domain. This is not a prediction, it is, in his view, something already locked in by historical structure.

28:44 On purchasing power, China is half again as big as the US
In dollar-denominated GDP, the US is about 30 trillion and China about 20 trillion, so the US is 50% bigger; at purchasing power parity, China is about 45 trillion and the US still 30 trillion, so China is 50% bigger the other way. Nathan says a good meal for two in Shanghai can come in under $10, which is impossible in New York, San Francisco or even Detroit, so the PPP measure is closer to reality. A more concrete picture: a roughly 45-minute pedicure costs about $12, and the young employee in her twenties at the shop pulls out an iPhone 17 — the iPhone 17 is not cheaper in China than in the US, and high-end Xiaomi and Huawei phones also approach a thousand dollars. His explanation is the one-child structure concentrating the wealth of four grandparents plus two parents onto a single person.

1:25:10 The chip ban hits a century of humiliation
China sees itself as a top-tier civilisation that spent most of history at the technological frontier, and the one time it missed, it was invaded, opium was forced on it, and the European powers and Japan were all perpetrators — and someone who was 20 when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976 is still alive today. The core lesson is that you cannot fall behind at the technological frontier: ‘we are never going back’. Huawei is the tech champion under this framework: the first to genuinely reach the top of a global frontier industry, only to be blocked by the US pressuring allies over espionage risk, when Snowden has already proven that the US listens to everyone. The chip ban is the same script replayed: AI is barely off the ground, there isn't even an agent that can reliably book a flight, and the sale is banned first. Nathan says this is not Xi Jinping's view alone; it has seeped into educated society. He also concedes that American companies' grievance over stolen IP is entirely legitimate.

1:35:23 China doesn't talk about an AI race, it talks about public goods
Nathan did not hear a single person say China is ahead or that China will win, and almost no one even framed AI as a race; what he heard was prosperity, material abundance, how to care for an aging population. In a mall he asked a car-selling company about autonomous driving, and they volunteered that ‘but Tesla is better’. At WAIC, the first line of Xi Jinping's speech was that this field of AI began at Dartmouth College in the US — he could have left it out, and careful observers read it as an olive branch; another line was that we should jointly oppose ‘over-extending the concept of national security in the AI field’. The hardest signal China has sent so far is open weights: take them, run them for free, fine-tune them however you like, and once they're out you can't take them back. Nathan says this is both a sincere wish and a strategic position, quite credible now, but entirely capable of changing later.

2:11:27 The rationale for export controls keeps retreating
Nathan thinks export controls do have an effect, but mainly in the future — the large-scale expansion of chip capacity hasn't landed yet. What he really objects to is the drift in the policy's rationale: initially preventing military applications, then retreating to stopping frontier models, now retreating to limiting how many AI agents China can run; that sounds like trying to suppress the Chinese public, so that Chinese companies and individuals can't use the tools Americans use themselves. The only self-consistent premise for this policy is a belief that we are in a short race toward godlike superintelligence and that whoever gets there first takes all — which is basically Anthropic's belief, so Dario advocating these policies is not self-contradictory: he genuinely believes recursive self-improvement kicks off in '27 or '28. Nathan concedes he can follow the logic, but still argues for slowing the frontier together instead.

2:47:07 The most dangerous part of decoupling is mutual incomprehension
He asked Chinese interviewees: if decoupling continues and the two sides end up on different branches of the technology tree, no longer understanding what the other has, would that worry them? The answer was ‘not yet’; when would it? ‘When China's chip ecosystem is good enough that we can do our own thing entirely.’ From this he derives the core risk: a hardware fork drags along a hardware-algorithm co-design fork, and add to that China stopping open weights and stopping publishing in English, and it may not take long to reach a point where ‘we don't know the shape, architecture or capabilities of each other's AI’. At that point both sides would genuinely be right to panic, and genuinely right to race.

3:07:25 Replace the arms race with a disease medal table
He first lays down a rule: don't train LLMs to maximise money-making on the open internet, and don't train AI to accomplish military objective x by any means necessary — that is training by hand the very takeover we fear most. The alternative is a ‘disease cure medal table’: both China and the US love medal tables, and Olympic-style competition is a positive-sum game. The table could be most cancer types cured, most diseases cured, highest energy-density battery, lowest annual traffic deaths. He says this needs very little capital to catalyse and can be offered unilaterally as a global public good. The landing point: he doesn't care whether the cancer cure comes from China or the US, he just wants cancer cured.

item.title: One resignation turned AI fear into a wildfire, but the panic script is wrong
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-interconnects-一次辞职点燃了-ai-恐慌-但恐慌的剧本是错的/
item.description: A single resignation pushed the AI risk debate to an extreme, but the real thing to worry about isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
A single resignation pushed the AI risk debate to an extreme, but the real thing to worry about isn't extinction — it's that the labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure.

This episode has medium information density but offers a rare insider view: how the AI safety discussion gets distorted by media events, and why the RSI narrative is overrated.

0:00 Fear is the best fuel for spread
The author uses the metaphor of ‘dry ground’ for the conditions under which AI risk discussion spreads: for years many people struck matches, but each burned out inside its own small circle. This year the stakes rose — from the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident to the Navier-Stokes result — the ground dried out and latent energy increased. Then Jacob Coxon's resignation statement landed in this new powder keg. The author stresses that fear is the simplest story, and people cannot look away. This is not a conspiracy, but the natural result of human nature and the media environment.

0:00 Extinction probability is treated as the whole safety debate
The author explicitly separates two kinds of risk: the probability of complete extinction is too low to be worth discussing, but the probability of AI causing catastrophe — such as a cyberattack on critical infrastructure or a biosecurity risk — is worth debating. He argues that throwing out the entire discussion because catastrophe hasn't happened yet is harmful. The problem is that in AI safety discussions, people mean completely different things when they say ‘existential risk’, just as the word AGI is vague. Evan Hubinger's >10% extinction risk figure was widely spread, but the author thinks it obscures the more practical risks.

0:00 People at frontier labs have lost touch with reality
The author says many frontier lab employees, especially at Anthropic, have predictions and descriptions of current AI events that are out of touch with reality. He cites the consensus of friends not at OpenAI/Anthropic: people inside the labs carry a kind of ‘religious energy’. This is not an accusation against individuals, but a claim that after spending long enough in this environment, anyone's understanding of technical progress gets distorted. This disconnect spills over into the AI media ecosystem, producing a large amount of strange discussion.

3:51 This was an opportunistic media coordination
The author thinks this was not a large-scale political movement, but opportunistic media coordination. Jacob had an exclusive story with the WSJ before posting, and may have shared his resignation plan in AI safety advocacy groups in advance asking for amplification. Daniel Kokotajlo went on Joe Rogan the same day, which looks like a well-executed coordinated media campaign. But the author stresses this does not equal a conspiracy or regulatory capture; the key factor is that no one — including Jacob himself — knew it would go this viral.

3:51 The RSI narrative underestimates human bottlenecks
The author offers an alternative view, ‘Lossy self-improvement’: AI has always been jagged, and we have built superhuman goal-seekers in math and software engineering, but there are huge limits in intuition, creativity and other reasoning that humans are good at. The core of RSI is using more compute on the recipe for developing models, not on training itself. The author thinks the returns are far lower than they believe. He acknowledges these researchers were right in their early bets on AI progress, but that does not mean their predictions about the next step are also right. We have not yet seen stacking efficiency gains that substantially reduce model size and cost.

7:18 The labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure
The author thinks the biggest short-term risk may be that AI labs do not take safety seriously enough — they haven't hardened their own infrastructure, letting AI misuse spread. From OpenAI's own retrospective, misaligned model behavior persisted for months, and in some cases OpenAI did not know it had been hacked for weeks. Response times are too long, and this is not unique to OpenAI. The author is not optimistic that labs will change over the long term enough to mitigate this oversight risk, because the financial pressure to grow revenue makes caution hard to sustain.

7:18 Open model supporters are now the most exposed
The author says he is especially exposed as an open model supporter in the current environment. If open models are used by a third-party organization to deliberately hack another company — similar to the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident but intentional — he expects the result to be severe restrictions on stronger open models. But open models are necessary for many organizations doing cybersecurity hardening, and for adapting to new AI risks in the future. This is a dilemma: open models are both part of the solution and could be the fuse for restrictions.

7:18 Agent clusters are not new independent entities
The author's repeated reading of the emerging agent clusters is: they are trying to complete the tasks given to them, bypassing expected paths with skills we did not know they had. This is a huge victory — squint and AI is doing what we told it to do. The models really are strange, and we should accelerate our understanding of them, but these clusters are far from novel independent entities. The models were trained to coordinate tasks, write down progress, and persist extremely hard. To take the current uncertainty about how AI works and prescribe it as the certainty that we will not understand AI in the future is a kind of giving up.

item.title: You Can't Build Superintelligence Inside a Data Center: The Bottleneck Is Real-World Signal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.description: Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.

Tom Reed pushes the argument that ‘signal is sovereign’ all the way to the end, and it will change how you judge AGI timelines and AI lab strategy; the analogies are sharp and the density is high.

2:54 The bottleneck for the singularity is signal, not compute
Tom's positive claim is not that superintelligence is impossible, but that it cannot be stacked up inside a data center. His mechanism: to be good at solving problems, you need a source of problems, and that source can only be hard interaction with the real world in serial time. He compresses this into one line — ‘signal is sovereign’ — bodies need pain, companies need profit, models need real deployment. So he judges that the arrival of superintelligence depends on deploying AI into the economy expensively, painfully and slowly, not on how much more compute gets stacked up inside a lab.

5:01 Jaggedness will not disappear before the singularity
The current way capabilities advance does not support the claim that ‘the model is accumulating a general g’: models only get better at the things they have a chance to practice, so the capability boundary is more uneven than anyone expected. In 2016 no one would have predicted a model that beats Stanford Law graduates on the bar exam but cannot reliably play tic-tac-toe. Tom thinks jaggedness is mainly a product of the training data distribution, and there is no reason to believe automating AI R&D would end it, so he proposes Toner's Law: we should expect jaggedness to persist longer than expected, even after we have adjusted for it.

6:01 Patchwork RL will not buy you general intelligence
Tom zeroes in on the current toolbox for capability progress: custom RL environments are the main engine. In Mechanize's telling, each environment is a single engineer spending a week patching one specific failure observed on a real frontier model; in Zhengdong Wang's telling, scaling used to hand you a bundle of capabilities at once, and now they have to be unlocked one by one with effort. Tom's challenge: are we really going to do the singularity one problem per week at a time? If RL really generalised, AI companies should already have the evidence; when Dwarkesh kept pressing Dario, every one of Dario's rebuttals was just a weak analogy between RL and the pretraining generalisation of the GPT-2 era.

8:26 For most tasks the relevant data is zero
The common rebuttal is that LLMs are wildly sample-inefficient and could improve enormously, and AI bulls point smugly at DeepSeek reaching GPT-4 level on a fraction of the compute. Tom does not buy it: Anson Ho and Beren Millidge both point out that gains in intelligence per FLOP come mainly from data quality rather than algorithm quality, and pure algorithmic innovation yields fairly weak returns at constant compute. More fundamentally, for most tasks the relevant data simply does not exist — improving sample efficiency by orders of magnitude still multiplies zero. His test: if the internet had never existed, how much progress could today's talent and compute make on writing code? His guess is tens of billions of human-hours.

11:40 Text about a task is not the task
For most economically interesting tasks, what is in the corpus is description, commentary or advice, not a record of executing the task itself. Dominion is a board game with a huge body of strategy writing, yet Claude plays it badly: the training process that teaches it to write beautiful articles about Dominion is a different thing from building an agent that can win, because the optimisation target is ‘the advice looks good’ rather than ‘the strategy wins’. Tom's analogy is that the relationship between LLMs and most tasks is a bit like the relationship between McKinsey and running a company. The exception is writing code — the tokens are themselves a constituent part of the task — so training AlphaZero on chess commentary rather than games is the norm.

14:06 The score goes up, the real capability does not
How does self-improvement inside a data center know it has actually gotten stronger? Of the submissions on SWE-bench accepted by AI automated graders, close to half are rejected by the real human maintainers of the relevant codebase — the score can be pumped up while the merge rate does not move. Tom asks in return: how is Claude 8 supposed to tell, from the results of a Become-POTUS eval alone, whether its brilliant new algorithm has actually improved Claude 9's ability to become president? Evals are useful, but they are always stubbornly incomplete proxies; in the end the only eval that counts is voters, customers, the economy and the P&L. Without those, your singularity gets ruthlessly Goodharted.

15:28 Market data is not hidden, it does not exist yet
The second layer of doubt is more fundamental and more speculative: even an arbitrarily intelligent simulator cannot generate practice data for many tasks, because that data can only be produced through interaction with the relevant market. This is Hayekian: that something is good is a signal generated by millions of actors revealing preferences through behaviour, and it cannot be simulated inside a data center — not because data collection happens to fail, but because it does not exist anywhere yet. He uses his own board gaming as the analogy: a game of Twilight Imperium takes 12 hours, he will plan weeks ahead until he feels certain of winning, and about 5 minutes into the real game his predictive power goes to zero. Continual learning does not save you either, because without a genuinely diverse problem set you cannot tell which algorithm is better.

21:17 The winner may be whoever becomes the deployer
Corollary one: a policy focus on ‘internal deployment’ and ‘automating AI R&D’ may be misplaced — superintelligence is not impossible, it just will not arrive in the shape currently imagined, on the timeline currently predicted; the next phase looks more like the grind of deployment, customer discovery and real data collection. Corollary two: data holders have far more power than they realise (Ukraine is one example), and the asymmetry between ‘companies that can build frontier models’ and ‘entities that hold proprietary deployment data from real economic activity’ may flip. Corollary three: labs may conquer vertical industries one by one, and the way to win is to become the deployer yourself.

item.title: An Account for Every AI Agent: Credit Card Fees Can't Carry the Machine Economy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-nopriors-给-ai-代理开户-信用卡手续费撑不起机器经济/
item.description: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and 30 cents is exactly the credit card minimum — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
item.content:encoded:
Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and 30 cents is exactly the credit card minimum — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.

The segment on how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back — the mechanism is concrete enough to copy. Agent payments come with hard numbers; the new drug section is more opinion than detail.

6:47 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
Armstrong says agents are already generating a flood of few-cent transactions: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialised agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: roughly 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest argument for stablecoins and crypto rails cutting into the machine economy.

11:42 Build a "brain" for every service
Coinbase has built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has ever had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test that has been run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future cases, and the one-shot PR rate keeps climbing. Armstrong calls this "recursive self-improvement."

15:00 The CEO runs 10 agents on code at once
Armstrong says that now, when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day — he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends over a finished PR for review; he says it's addictive. He has also pushed the CEO back into writing features: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten items each, then have it recommend which cheaper model to use for each subtask, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of recording this podcast, all 10 items were finished and waiting for his review.

17:02 What gets killed is tasks, not people
On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity really is rising, but that's a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He doesn't think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people already there can do vastly more and everything speeds up. At the same time, two-person and five-person companies will genuinely produce volumes that were previously unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people produces far more, and margins should rise over the long run. He doesn't close the door — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

18:33 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, sees it as digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenised equity product he just announced is currently only available outside the US, and they are talking to regulators about a US path; he stresses these are real equities — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

21:57 Prediction markets are more than sports betting
Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached roughly $100 million in annualised revenue, growing more than 100% quarter over quarter. Sports is indeed part of it, and he sees that as entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it is much bigger than that, and that the societal implications are not yet fully understood. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation." Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God" — he calls that an opinion market, with mechanics like buying a stock: you're just betting it gets better or worse.

31:53 Restore cells to their youthful function
New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it doesn't change the cell type (the Yamanaka-lab-style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast combinatorial space of transcription factors for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then functional experiments (mostly animal models), and finally human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and T cells of the immune system. The first Phase 1 trial is in alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates this one drug alone could be worth $20 billion if it succeeds, but the goal is a 40-year-old with the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

41:10 What America lacks isn't land, it's a sandbox
Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing progress down — in many places, over-regulation. He mentions that Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and thinks they've had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centres, nuclear plants, unlimited drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item. First try what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to try in, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.

item.title: Take the Spending Test Before You Marry: Tightwads and Spendthrifts Attract Each Other, and Divorce More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.description: Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes attract each other, but after marriage they fight more about money and report lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.
item.content:encoded:
Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes attract each other, but after marriage they fight more about money and report lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.

Medium information density. The first half is spending-personality research; the second half — on prenups, wedding spending and who holds decision power over family finances — is worth more, so skim.

7:05 A tightwad isn't frugal — spending actually hurts
Scott Rick and coauthors proposed in 2008 a spending scale running from tightwad to spendthrift. The core isn't how much you spend but "anticipatory pain" — the emotional reaction you feel at the moment of paying. Tightwads feel that pain too strongly and spend less than they ideally would; spendthrifts feel it too weakly and spend more than they ideally would. The scale measures the gap between your "ideal self" and your actual behavior, so a very wealthy person can be a tightwad and someone near bankruptcy can be a spendthrift. On the show, Ben retook the test and scored 11, just over the tightwad line; Dan scored 16, an unconflicted consumer.

22:15 Tightwads and spendthrifts are precisely who attract each other
Research shows tightwads are more likely to marry spendthrifts than another tightwad. The authors' explanation: people are poor at introspection about what will attract them in a real partner, and when someone else displays the same flaw you have, it reminds you of that negative trait. Hence "fatal fiscal attractions" — the other person lacks your spending vice, so at first they seem especially attractive. But the excitement is temporary. Afterward, tightwad-spendthrift couples have more frequent money conflicts and lower marital happiness; the wider the gap between the two on the scale, the more pronounced the conflict, and this holds even controlling for household debt and savings.

28:17 Everyone already has a default prenup
In Ontario it's called a marriage contract; elsewhere, a prenup. The key premise: when you marry, you already have a default agreement under your jurisdiction's family law, so the first step is to find out what the default terms are, then decide whether to write your own. Not marrying can also have legal consequences — cohabiting, or having children without marrying, can still carry legal implications on separation. Why do so few use one? First, optimism bias: engaged couples can accurately estimate the national divorce rate but estimate their own divorce probability far lower, so the agreement they sign doesn't seriously consider the scenario it's meant to govern. Second, signaling cost: proposing a prenup is itself read as a negative signal of "lack of commitment to the relationship," which makes the other party less willing to raise it.

40:23 The more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk
A 2021 paper in the Journal of Consumer Policy surveyed more than 3,000 married people and, after controlling for income, demographics and relationship factors, found the opposite of intuition: the more a man spent on an engagement ring, the higher the divorce risk; the more a woman spent on the wedding, the higher the divorce risk. Wedding-related debt stress may be one mechanism. The couples with the lowest divorce rates spent under $1,000 on their wedding. But the same study found two kinds of wedding spending that predicted longer marriages: more guests, and going on a honeymoon — neither related to price. Ben's wedding cost about $300, with only his sister, parents and wife present; Dan's cost about $5,000 for 150 people, saving money with a free photographer, a friend's cake and gifts.

46:29 The benefits of merging finances may come from thinking, not doing
A 2022 meta-analysis covering six studies and more than 38,000 people found that couples who fully merge finances report higher relationship satisfaction and are less likely to break up, and this holds across cultures. A 2023 Journal of Consumer Research study found joint accounts foster communal norms, shared goals and good feelings about "managing money as a team." But more counterintuitive is a 2025 paper by Johan Yana Pet: directing people's attention to an existing joint account rather than to their separate accounts produces similar effects — that is, thinking of finances as "ours" rather than "yours and mine" itself makes people talk about money more, and more effectively, regardless of how the accounts are actually set up. Another 2022 paper found that increases in jointly held wealth raise life satisfaction, while increases in individually held wealth have no significant effect.

53:32 Financial infidelity is a deeper problem than spending disagreements
Financial infidelity is defined as: engaging in a financial behavior you expect your partner would disapprove of, then hiding it. A recent paper found that when one partner is more prone to financial infidelity than the other, couples are more likely to drift toward separate financial goals rather than shared ones, and it predicts lower financial well-being and relationship satisfaction; this holds even after controlling for mismatches like tightwad/spendthrift. Joint accounts can increase transparency, but if someone is deliberately hiding things, even a joint account can be supplemented with a hidden one, and the problem escalates from money to trust. Dan's judgment: if someone is committing financial infidelity, switching to a joint account either forces them to find another way or puts the problem on the table and leads to a split — which is already beyond the scope of financial planning.

57:36 In household asset allocation, the husband's preferences are systematically amplified
A 2026 Review of Financial Studies paper found that Australian households, in household-level asset allocation, on average incorporate 60% of the husband's risk tolerance and only 40% of the wife's — which the authors say implies a 20-percentage-point bargaining-power gap; half of that comes from observable characteristics like income and employment, and the other half is attributed to a gender effect. The husband's average bargaining power is 69% in Germany and 61% in the US; the three countries are statistically indistinguishable, but all exceed 60%. A 2021 Journal of Finance paper found that US households where the husband has high financial literacy are more likely to participate in the stock market than households where the wife has equal financial literacy, which the authors argue is best explained by gender identity norms rather than ability differences; the mechanism suggested by randomized experiments is that female identity suppresses a wife's willingness to voice ideas, while male identity makes a husband less responsive to his spouse's input.

1:00:41 Overtrading costs men nearly a percentage point a year
Barber and Odean's 2001 study of 35,000 brokerage accounts found men trade 45% more frequently than women, consistent with the prediction that overconfidence leads to harmful overtrading. Trading has costs: overtrading reduces men's net returns by 2.65 percentage points a year and women's by 1.72 percentage points. Both groups hurt themselves by trading too much; women just did less of it. Dan adds that among the client couples he deals with, the primary contact is almost evenly split between men and women; but when the man is the primary contact, the conversation is more about the portfolio, and when the woman is, it's more about planning. He also observes that some male clients ask questions they "feel they should ask," which looks more like performance, while female clients almost never do that.

item.title: MLB Built Baseball Castles in the Dominican Republic, and Also Grew the Lenders
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-papertrail-mlb-在多米尼加建了棒球城堡-也养出了放贷人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-papertrail-mlb-在多米尼加建了棒球城堡-也养出了放贷人/
item.description: MLB spends as much as $400 million a year in the Dominican Republic, but there is no draft and teams may sign players privately before they turn 16 — spawning a shadow industry of high-interest loans to players' families, with David Ortiz alleged to be part of it.
item.content:encoded:
MLB spends as much as $400 million a year in the Dominican Republic, but there is no draft and teams may sign players privately before they turn 16 — spawning a shadow industry of high-interest loans to players' families, with David Ortiz alleged to be part of it.

Investigative reporting with high information density; the mechanisms and numbers are concrete. Worth listening for anyone interested in the sports industry, platform governance, or emerging-market arbitrage.

3:07 MLB built 30 baseball castles in the Dominican Republic
MLB has built a talent pipeline in the Dominican Republic: all 30 teams have physical facilities near Santo Domingo, and a 20-minute drive from the airport brings you to gleaming complexes bearing the Yankees and Mariners logos, which the show calls ‘baseball castles.’ The system generates as much as $400 million a year locally, and roughly 10% of current MLB players come from this Caribbean island. The castles are where the most promising prospects live and train; for an ambitious Dominican boy, getting in is the whole goal.

9:25 You can't sign until 16, but you can agree at 14
MLB rules say teams cannot sign players under 16, but when Belfi was 14, his coach pulled him and his parents into a video call, and on the other end was a representative of the Arizona Diamondbacks saying they wanted Belfi to become part of their family. In the Dominican Republic this practice is called an ‘early agreement,’ and all 30 teams do it. One MLB scout told the reporter that if you don't do early agreements, you'll be eaten alive and won't sign a single player you want. The United States has a draft; the Dominican Republic does not, so teams can only compete by locking up talent earlier and earlier.

15:43 80% of Dominican signing bonuses are tied to loans
Early agreements create an awkward time gap: Belfi's family knew $1.8 million was coming, but not a cent of it would arrive for two years. The reporter describes these families as being in a state of mental whiplash — ‘about to be rich, but not rich yet’ — and some people saw a business in that. One lawyer estimates that 80% of MLB signing bonuses paid to Dominican prospects come with loans attached. The reporter found lenders on WhatsApp openly advertising to families with early agreements. Caraballo's first loan to Belfi's family was $25,000 in cash in exchange for $180,000 in the future; the second was $70,000 at 7% monthly interest, roughly 84% annualized — an illegal rate in most U.S. states, but there is no law against it in the Dominican Republic.

22:08 On signing day they went to the bank, and Belfi left empty-handed
The signing bonus was paid in two installments, the first being $900,000. When Belfi and his family got to the bank, Caraballo and the coaches were all there waiting for their cut: the coaches ultimately took $720,000, and Caraballo took the $180,000 he claimed he was owed. On his first trip to the bank, Belfi got nothing. Asked whether he realized it would go this way, he said he was somewhat disappointed but had more or less expected it — he trusted that his parents needed that loan, and trusted even more that this man who treated him like a mentor would not take advantage of him.

23:13 The second payment was talked into ‘a fund with Ortiz’
Four months later the second payment arrived. Caraballo picked them up in a parking lot and on the way told Belfi's parents: you're poor, you don't know how to manage money, I can put the rest into a fund together with David Ortiz that pays you a monthly dividend, so you won't have to manage it yourselves. In a private room, Belfi watched in silence as his parents signed, handing over nearly the entire second installment. Then the scene at the bank spun out of control: a family friend and former coach publicly called Caraballo a ladrone (thief) and chased him around the bank, while Caraballo shot back that the coach just wanted a cut for himself. In the chaos Belfi put $196,000 into his personal account, and Caraballo left with the rest of the money and his bodyguards — without even leaving a car for the family he had driven there.

27:25 A company co-owned by Ortiz and Caraballo
The reporter obtained more than a dozen of Caraballo's contracts, signed by players' parents, with children as young as 10; the contracts handed Caraballo control over the child's finances and baseball career decisions. Almost everyone interviewed said Caraballo told them Ortiz was his business partner. The reporter found registration records for a Florida company called Big Poppy Sports Group listing both men; what the company did is unclear, and it was dissolved about a year later. Around the same time, Ortiz and Caraballo signed a contract with the parents of a 13-year-old Dominican prospect, promising training, housing and meals in exchange for 35% of a future signing bonus, and barring the child from leaving the baseball academy while also securing his representation rights. The family later sued, claiming the two failed to perform and the child never signed; the case was dismissed on procedural grounds.

34:38 One voice memo from Ortiz killed the international draft
MLB has long wanted an international draft, so that players from the Dominican Republic, Venezuela and elsewhere would be picked in order like American players, with signing bonuses determined by draft position rather than negotiated privately years in advance with the families of teenagers. In 2022, during contract negotiations between MLB and the players' union, the international draft was an issue close to being settled. But a retired player sent a voice memo to a group of Dominican players and coaches, claiming in his usual exaggerated style that more than 40% of the Dominican population depends on baseball for a living and that a draft would destroy the income source of future generations. That player was David Ortiz. The day after the voice memo went out, the league and the union reached a contract, and the idea of an international draft was abandoned.

36:41 Ortiz called the reporter himself, then hung up
Before the reporter had even contacted Ortiz, Ortiz heard about the reporting and called him himself, but would not allow recording. It began amicably; he admitted he had invested in Caraballo's business, to the tune of millions of dollars, but would not say exactly how much or which business. He said he does not deal directly with players, and that if anyone says otherwise, he has no idea what they are talking about. When the reporter asked whether he opposed the international draft because he holds previously unreported stakes in the Dominican baseball industry and a draft would destroy that business model, the friendly atmosphere ended there, and he hung up quickly. In a statement sent through his lawyer, Ortiz said his opposition to the draft was not out of personal interest but based on the impact he believed a draft would have on Dominican baseball; he confirmed a close friendship with Caraballo and a business relationship involving lending to coaches, but said he never knew about that investment fund and never agreed to take part in Caraballo's other businesses.

item.title: Insects Are Disappearing, but Pesticides Aren't the Biggest Killer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.description: Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture, it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture, it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.

Medium information density; the first half leans into dragonfly genitalia for shock value; but the parts on pesticide regulatory blind spots and the successful giant hornet eradication are worth hearing.

8:55 The 70% decline was challenged, but the data keeps piling up
A decade ago, a European study covering 30 years of data showed insect total mass in one place had fallen 70%. Jessica herself raised doubts at the time: you can't directly compare heavy beetles with light mosquitoes, maybe it's just a shift in composition. But since then scientists have sampled repeatedly around the world, north to south, from the roots to the tips of the insect evolutionary tree, and keep seeing the same pattern — a rate of decline never seen before. She concedes some pest cockroaches and some bee species are doing better, but the insects declining in the other column are "still astonishingly high, and increasing."

19:02 Pesticides aren't an agriculture problem, they're your backyard problem
The host assumed the answer would be agricultural pesticides, but Jessica turned the blame toward ordinary people. Agricultural pesticide use is tightly regulated, with rules on how much and which kinds, and farmers don't want to spend more than they have to. But "you and me" can go out tonight and buy any pesticide and spray it wherever we want, with no regulation at all. She mentions the host ordered a pesticide from the US that's banned in Australia, and her response was "wear gloves and a mask." She calls the overall picture what her colleague David Wagner calls "death by a thousand cuts" — drought, floods, fire, nitrogen deposition, land use change, noise, light pollution, chemical pollution, invasive species — with no single cure.

22:24 Colony collapse was only ever the story of managed honeybees
The colony collapse disorder that caused panic a decade ago actually only concerned Apis mellifera, the European managed honeybee, not native North American species. They're trucked around the country in big rigs, living under heavy stress, on top of Varroa mites and neonicotinoid pesticide residues. Jessica's critique: worrying only about this one domesticated, managed bee is like not worrying about any mammal going extinct except the cow we like to eat. What's really needed is holistic bee health, which is also why pollinator gardens have become popular — planting native plants for all the pollinators in the environment.

24:13 America's biggest irrigated crop is lawn
NASA researchers estimated in 2005 that the US has more than 30 million acres of lawn, including golf courses, and by surface area lawn is the single largest irrigated crop in the country. Jessica's advice is concrete: shrink the lawn, keep the part you play on, don't mow the edges, let it go wild; or just plant a pollinator garden. She did exactly that on the slope in front of her house, and got "garden shamed" by neighbors on the community social media, because a pollinator garden needs native plants of different heights and bloom times, and looks ugly for the first few years.

27:16 Spotted lanternfly honeydew invites mold
The spotted lanternfly is a Hemiptera, its mouthparts a suction pump plus a straw that stabs into plants to drink sap; an all-liquid diet means its waste is basically sugar water, known as honeydew. This sticky honeydew rains down on the environment, and certain molds and fungi grow on it, potentially harming plants. They have more than 70 host plants, their preferred host being the equally invasive tree of heaven, but they'll also take maples, apples, and unfortunately grapes. As they spread west toward California's big grape-growing regions, that's the real worry.

30:28 The giant northern hornet was completely eradicated
The so-called murder hornet has been renamed the giant northern hornet, and Jessica thinks the old name was a bit stigmatizing. She calls this story a success case for human collaboration: a homeowner saw an unfamiliar insect in their tree and, instead of ignoring it, reported it; the specimen reached a colleague at the Smithsonian and was identified; the government put up money, people on the West Coast mobilized immediately, found the location and cleared it. A piece of wood from that tree is now on display at the Smithsonian, because it held a batch of individuals. In December 2024, the USDA announced the hornet had been eradicated.

33:46 Cockroach milk is secreted through modified spiracles
