Most cockroaches lay egg cases called oothika, which look like little coffee beans; when they hatch, all the larvae take a breath at once and pop the "little box" open. But cockroaches like diploptera punctata are ovoviviparous, and the mother feeds the embryos a milk-like secretion. Insects aren't mammals and have no nipples, so they modified spiracles to secrete this milk. Compositionally it's high in protein, not all that different from mammalian milk, and cloudy white in color. A few years ago European scientists tried to pitch it as the next superfood. The current problem: extracting the milk usually means sacrificing the mother.

37:36 Fear of bugs is learned from your mother
Jessica says fear of insects is learned, not innate. A colleague at Rutgers ran an experiment: put babies and tarantulas together, and the babies aren't afraid on their own; but if the mother or primary caregiver shows disgust, the baby shows disgust too. Same with snakes and other animals. She uses her own two kids as an example: her daughter didn't start daycare until nearly one and was never afraid of bugs; her son started daycare at six weeks, and the daycare teacher was afraid of bugs and would scream and try to swat them, so her son grew up afraid of bugs — even though his own mother isn't. Once this learned behavior forms, it's very hard to change.

item.title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.description: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the unaugmented able-bodied minority become the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a complaint — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
item.content:encoded:
Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the unaugmented able-bodied minority become the "original sinners" who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a complaint — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.

Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; its value is in the concrete scenes and in how a single play grew. Anyone looking for methodology or industry judgment can skip it.

7:15 Disabled women being unable to leave the house is a widespread phenomenon
Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Han Ya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of the sisters had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives during holidays, her feeling was that it was "like walking a little dog or cat." Later she got her first computer, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. After getting the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another visually impaired mother was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, saying "you can't see, you can't raise a child"; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These oral accounts made Yaoyao realize that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

11:19 Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only find friends who also use wheelchairs; they hung bags all over the chairs and hauled load after load. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would be done in half a day. The colleague was stunned for a moment and said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she didn't have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao said she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and only realized one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people don't even have a chance to meet, "you have no chance of integration at all." This was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

14:19 Writing able-bodied people as the discriminated original sinners
The Leyi troupe's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), does a direct identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans after technological modification like electronic eyes and cochlear implants; the remaining able-bodied minority, because of "the crime of starting the nuclear war," become original sinners marginalized by society. Yaoyao's logic was that since she herself is a situs inversus person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights able-bodied people have to fight for — she calls this writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The core of the plot: an original-sinner father, to keep his son from suffering because of his able-bodied body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to saw off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes bring out the discussion of original sinners and augmented humans.

22:25 How the unseen and the unheard partner up
Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition to be his partner. His first reaction was confusion: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace signs, tapping once when it was Wang's turn to speak. Director Ma Yan said that abroad there is already a form of blind and deaf performers on stage together, with the deaf person's hand on the visually impaired person's hand so the latter can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin said he had been around deaf people since childhood, but back then he thought these were two kinds of people born with communication barriers, "absolutely impossible to communicate," and the barrier was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time subtitle screens, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

25:28 Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact "cheating": they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and then delivered them smoothly on stage, so the director had no way to assess them and only wondered how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language and could only watch everyone signing while laughing on the side, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign language. Once they got familiar, everyone knew each other's little tricks.

30:36 She received the Best Play award in the ICU
In 2024 Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and a friend stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while other groups' tables were empty and everyone was dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking "how could it possibly be us." In the end they won Best Play, the highest award of the Nanjing New Theatre Festival, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. At the same moment the news reached the ICU, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. In October of the same year the play was specially invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, as the first disability-integrated play and the only production in the "Nothing Is Impossible" section.

35:45 After writing this play, she changed her answer and chose not to be born
The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health status and family environment, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families, there are deaf parents who must truthfully tell their child you will also be deaf when you are born, a husband who deceives his wife into having a child, a family that favors boys over girls, and the last story is adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script because their life experiences were so similar, only the illnesses differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if given another chance, most in the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; but Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society with no choice.

36:45 The same question, Cai Cong and she give opposite answers
The program contrasts the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born with the real-life Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see if the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting just because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give the child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and debate around this choice persists. The program's question is: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have?

item.title: Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in nematodes; in humans there is no evidence yet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.description: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.
item.content:encoded:
Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in nematodes, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.

35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with experimental designs and key numbers included; on the mammalian part the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so it won't hand you a conclusion you can apply.

4:37 The genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out one page
Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's analogy is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out just one page, and that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of the RNA that gets transcribed does other things, many of which remain unexplained. This distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and only then does the question become whether lived experience can rewrite those instructions.

11:35 Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
Why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for the erasure is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being locked into the few pieces one room happened to make.

12:46 It was opposed and desired, and not entirely for data reasons
This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is theory, the barrier is simply there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He gives Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he doesn't push this into ‘because people want to believe it, it has promise’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

16:20 Nematodes can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
Why should you trust nematodes? The conditions Rechavi lists are concrete: a C. elegans is always 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, raised in a dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; the generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run hundreds of generations of nematodes. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in nematodes already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

21:20 Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses
The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the nematode turns green, while if it is destroyed it stays black. First let nematodes be infected by the virus and destroy it, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in their offspring — these offspring have no ability to make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still turn black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happens: all the offspring are black, and the resistance can be passed on for several more generations. Sequencing can directly read those small RNAs matching the viral genome, and only the offspring of infected parents have them. These nematodes have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

24:46 The brain and heredity don't use the same language
The boldest question in this episode is: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out that the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something might just mean removing a particular odorant receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been proven convincingly enough, because no one has explained how information travels from the brain to the germline. His own route bypasses translation: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of naturally occurring small RNAs in the nematode brain altered the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them all the way to three generations later, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

28:17 Mammals lack an RNA amplifier
Why can nematodes do it while mammals must be doubted? The mechanism Rechavi gives is blunt: the nematode's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: when there are only a few cells, perhaps even acting on the placenta formed during pregnancy, and then step by step it steers development off course, with problems like metabolism following. This is the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ line of thinking. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, and time will tell’.

31:07 RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
The applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples planning to have children get DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but right now no one looks at RNA; if the mechanism becomes clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, and certain RNAs might be associated with disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. Only a step beyond that comes intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if the mice are made to exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; during IVF you might be able to change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it were figured out, he has imagined telling someone preparing for IVF ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, and that would change your RNA profile.

item.title: Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail, and Retail Theft Is Now an Industry
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant bring in only about a third.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Connected goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant bring in only about a third.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation, with plenty of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious, which Scott describes as the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years: of malicious shrink, about 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only within a few points each year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that they have been underreported ever since COVID, with neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capturing it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal, and these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to trade for money — so they will get physical, and they have. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and some have been killed. So asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene, just to back off. His attitude: he will trade shrink for human safety every single day, and management and the board will back that decision.

23:53 RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and is still expensive and hard to scale in 2026. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, essentially a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read and only actively transmitting solutions work. He also says tag cost is now almost zero, and the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely expensive. They have tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but retrofitting an entire production line for a single drill is very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs to go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — maybe a garage, a warehouse, or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately understand it's a gross margin problem — as long as it breaks even or even makes a little money, locking it up pencils out. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and when they break a bit on the job site and rush to the store only to find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up carefully selected categories, with a QR code to summon an associate who unlocks it in an average of 90 seconds; and locking things up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the product is finally in stock.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can drive the goods right out
In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where a whole container is rerouted at the port or a transload warehouse and hauled somewhere else, sometimes even loaded back onto a container ship and sailed away; second, a driver crosses state lines on an eight-hour run, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, made to look real with AI, where a driver pulls in, says he's picking up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new isn't necessarily the methods but the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years, with trains sitting in a yard getting cracked open by a group of people; and the other side has good intelligence, hitting not every car but only the one carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 In security, AI is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency problem: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores so existing cameras can run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a specific combination of suspicious behaviors and then recognize the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago no one cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he is very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan cosponsors, it has passed the House, and it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, with the president saying he will sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources, and the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: no one took it seriously, and the prevailing mood then was decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Baseball's stadium music isn't accompaniment — it's how fans take the game back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.description: Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the visiting pitcher — music turns the crowd from spectators into part of the game.
item.content:encoded:
Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the visiting pitcher — music turns the crowd from spectators into part of the game.

Medium information density: the first half is baseball music history, and only the Nancy Faust story in the back half is worth the price. Worth listening for anyone into sports, live experience, or fan culture.

0:00 One walk-up song can turn a passerby into a fan
Host Randa Abdel Fattah says she was indifferent to baseball for most of her life, until Mets pitcher Edwin Diaz's walk-up song Narco changed that in 2022. Diaz is a closer, usually entering at a key moment in the late innings, and the team uses his walk-up song to announce to the opponent that the fun is over and this one is theirs. The entrance video went viral, the team started handing out plastic trumpets to fans, the mascots Mr. and Mrs. Met pretended to play trumpets, and eventually the team flew the original artist, Timmy Trumpet, in from Australia to perform live. The host says that if you were in the stands at that moment, the feeling was electric.

6:18 The official historian finds the ballpark too loud
MLB's official historian John Thorne says plainly that he doesn't like entrance music. What he misses is the quiet between half-innings — quiet that lets other sounds ring out louder and clearer: the strange sound of a bat hitting a baseball, the same sound when Babe Ruth hit and when Josh Gibson hit; the dull thud of a leather glove catching a fly ball; a coach yelling at a player to keep running and steal second. He thinks nonstop audio and the endless fight for fans' attention may have robbed a kid who goes to the ballpark to dream of that right.

10:31 Take Me Out was originally a women's suffrage song
The seventh-inning stretch was originally literal: stand up, move your legs, get the blood flowing. It became a musical moment thanks to a 1908 song, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, which was actually about women's suffrage. The protagonist in the original lyrics is Katie Casey, a baseball fan who knows all the players' names, gets upset when the umpire makes a bad call, and knows what to do when the score is tight — she gets the whole crowd to sing along. From this came a whole new genre, the "baseball song," which flooded sheet music, cylinder records and 78s in the 1910s.

12:35 The baseball song boom was publishers, not fans
John Thorne points out that the 1910s wave of baseball music was less about fans liking it than about publishers liking it — it was essentially a marketing tool to pull people into the ballpark. The evidence is the number of copycats: George M. Cohan released Take Your Girl to the Ball Game almost the same week, followed by imitations like I Want to Go to the Ball Game. But despite all the baseball songs Tin Pan Alley produced, large-scale singing in actual ballparks remained rare, and John says the main reason was technical: sound systems were too primitive, and before radio took hold, a brass band was still the best accompaniment.

17:47 That 1977 singalong broke the visiting pitcher
On a muggy July night in Chicago in 1977, the White Sox were down two runs to the Kansas City Royals. After the White Sox put runners on first and second, people in the stands started singing Hey Hey Goodbye, the sound grew, more than 45,000 fans joined in, and the announcers had to raise their voices to be heard over the singing. The White Sox then erupted — bases loaded, bases cleared, four runs in — and the other side was forced to change pitchers. As the pitcher walked off the mound, Chicago fans sent him off even louder. Nancy Faust says she was thinking, "Did I hear that right?" because this wasn't the kind of thing you normally heard at a ballpark — it was more like mockery.

23:51 She gave players songs; fans fed her ideas
In her first years with the White Sox, Nancy Faust still played the established repertoire: the national anthem, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, and the hour when the crowd came in. In her third year she started improvising, playing whatever she saw. When Dick Allen came up, the crowd would leave the restrooms and popcorn stands, so she played the then-popular Jesus Christ Superstar, and when he hit a home run the place went crazy. Fans sitting around her booth started feeding her ideas: one player had worked at a watch counter, the store closed and he got stuck there, so when he came up she played Does Anybody Really Know What Time It Is. She says she was "the soundtrack to whatever was happening," not just a soundtrack for the players.

25:52 A visiting pitcher admitted the singing shook his confidence
After that 1977 singalong, a visiting pitcher told reporters: you're standing on the mound, there are men on base, Zisk is in the batter's box, thirty thousand people are singing Kiss It Goodbye, and that shakes your confidence. Nancy Faust later read in a book that players recalling those years said they hated hearing that sound and cringed at the na-na-goodbye. And White Sox slugger Richie Zisk said of those same fans: I don't know whether they came to see us or we came to see them, but I can tell you it got us fired up. Nancy's conclusion: I guess I did have an impact, I just didn't know it at the time.

28:56 She couldn't read music and did it all by ear
Every song Nancy Faust improvised over her career, she did by ear — she couldn't read music. Hum a few bars of anything and within seconds she could play it back on the organ. She retired from the White Sox organist job in 2010, White Sox fan and former president Barack Obama personally wrote to congratulate her on her career, and the booth where she spent decades is now named after her. She still occasionally comes back for special occasions, like Pope Night, playing Gotta Have Faith and Don't Stop Believing.

item.title: Iron Age Ireland had no Celtic invasion, only trade and language
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/

item.description: The traditional story says the Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.
item.content:encoded:
The traditional story says the Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.

Medium information density, with a long setup in the first half. The real value is in the second half, on Celtic identity, sacral kingship and the Fianna warband, suited to listeners interested in pre-Roman Europe.

2:18 Why the Irish Iron Age is the murkiest period
John Waddell says the Irish Iron Age is the darkest stretch of Irish prehistory, partly because people at the time cremated their dead. In much of Europe people were buried with large quantities of fine grave goods, whereas cremation plus burial destroys a great deal of useful archaeological evidence. So despite very fine metalwork and monuments, the absence of burial evidence makes this history especially hard to read. He also points out that using the phrase "Celtic Iron Age" to describe the period amounts to slapping an ethnic label on an era, adding another layer of trouble to an already complicated story.

9:28 Sea routes connected people rather than isolating them
Waddell repeatedly stresses an underrated fact: in prehistory, waterways were channels connecting people, not barriers. Ireland and Britain are both islands, and people habitually assume islands mean isolation, but coastal routes and river routes were very likely the main means of connection. Before the Romans built straight roads, travel by water was far easier than travel by land. This means we have consistently underestimated how connected the populations of prehistoric Britain and Ireland were. The Irish Sea itself was a connecting force, and the English Channel linked England to the continent.

10:31 Sacred sites sat on high ground, not by rivers
Tristan asks whether Iron Age settlements were all close to rivers and coasts. Waddell's answer is unexpected: famous sites like Tara, Rathcroghan and Navan Fort are not obviously on major routes. Each sits on high ground in its own different way, and these locations may have carried a kind of sanctity since the Neolithic. Tara was already an important burial place before 3000 BC, and its story runs into the medieval period, representing more than 4000 years of ritual activity. The importance of these places comes from accumulated time and religious meaning, not from rivers and sea routes.

15:38 A sacred king who fails or is wounded is deposed
Waddell reads a key concept out of medieval Irish texts: sacral kingship. The king of Tara was not a political strongman; his fundamental duty was to maintain cosmic order. If a sacred king could not bring good harvests, he was deposed. Another feature was that his body had to be flawless: once a sacred king was wounded, scarred or deformed, he was deposed. Waddell thinks this ritual may eventually be traceable in the archaeology of Britain and Ireland, suggesting that in the Celtic era, the pre-Roman period, certain tribal rulers did carry a sacred quality.

21:43 The Celts were not invaders but a language community
The traditional story is that around 500 BC, Celtic-speaking peoples brought knowledge of iron to Ireland. Waddell says this is wrong. His best definition of the ancient Celts is "people who spoke Celtic", not an ethnic or racial definition. Ireland in the pre-Roman period was undoubtedly Celtic-speaking, but archaeology finds almost no evidence of incoming migrants in the Iron Age or the Late Bronze Age. Instead, from about 1000 BC there is abundant archaeological evidence of trade and exchange between Britain and Ireland, with the Thames, the Rhine, the Rhône, the Saône, the Loire and the Danube all serving as major corridors. Trade and exchange means movement of people, and people carried myths, legends and language with them. The Celtic languages most likely took shape gradually amid this Late Bronze Age surge of connectivity.

31:04 The Banquet Hall is really a ritual processional way
On the hill of Tara there is a monument called the Banquet Hall, a pair of very long parallel earthworks. Waddell's colleague Conor Newman established that it was never a banquet hall — it is far too large to be any kind of hall. Standing between the banks, you find you cannot see the world outside, because the banks are still high even in their ruined state. Newman proposed that it was a processional way, running from the northern end of the hill to the centre of the summit, used for kingly inauguration rites. There are gaps in the banks that let the procession look left and right at the burials and other monuments on either side, reminding the man about to become sacred king of the stories of his ancestors and predecessors. Waddell compares it to Rome's Appian Way, lined on both sides with tombs.

33:07 Beneath Tara lies a timber circle bigger than Stonehenge
Geophysical survey on the hill of Tara revealed a huge circular timber structure, four to five times the scale of Stonehenge. It was built around 2000 BC and should have stood on the hilltop as prominently as Stonehenge, yet today there is no trace of it on the ground — only aerial photographs show the faint outline of the circle. Waddell says this reminds us that large timber circles earlier than Stonehenge are a feature of the prehistoric landscape of Britain and Ireland. Tara's burials have another detail: many of them intersect one another, as if new graves were deliberately laid partly over old ones to connect with ancestral remains, both legitimising one's own existence and conveying some kind of story.

39:22 The forgotten king Dathi and a Swiss myth
Waddell tells the story of an almost forgotten king, Dathi, associated with Rathcroghan in western Ireland. In medieval legend Dathi was the last pagan king of Ireland, said to have campaigned on the European continent, perhaps reaching the foot of the Swiss Alps, and to have been struck dead by lightning at the foot of the Alps, with his body carried back to Ireland and buried at Rathcroghan. The story was especially popular in the 19th century, because some people took it as proof that Irish military power reached far overseas. But Waddell says it looks like pure fabrication: there never was an Irish invasion of Switzerland. Dathi most likely only raided Britain occasionally. He was later overshadowed by the more famous warrior Cú Chulainn and gradually forgotten.

item.title: Ashurbanipal's Library: He Was Both a Tyrant and the Earliest Book Collector
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.
item.content:encoded:
Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.

Medium information density; the first half is Mesopotamian background, and the second half — how the library was preserved and deciphered — is where the value is.

0:01 The same man, two completely opposite first impressions
At the British Museum, Tracy read the exhibit panels on Ashurbanipal's library and thought, "this guy's library is astonishing"; in the same gallery Patrick read the other set of panels about him as the Assyrian king, and came away thinking, "this guy was really cruel." The same body of material can support two completely opposite impressions at once, and the rest of the episode picks apart that contradiction: he really did yoke the defeated Elamite king to his chariot and lock a rival in a dog kennel, and he really did order texts from across the empire copied and sent to the capital.

4:04 You simply cannot lay out a Mesopotamian timeline
Tracy wanted to open the episode with a basic timeline and found she couldn't. Mesopotamia spans more than three thousand years from the first cities, with civilizations, kingdoms and empires overlapping and influencing one another, so a linear timeline is itself a distortion. Assyrian history is divided into Early Assyrian (from about 2600 BCE), Old Assyrian (from about 2025 BCE), Middle Assyrian (from about 1363 BCE), and Neo-Assyrian (911 to 609 BCE), followed by a post-empire period. Assyrian people still exist today: roughly three to five million people in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey identify as Assyrian.

9:10 The father split the empire in two to prevent civil war
Esarhaddon's father Sennacherib had utterly destroyed Babylon and even diverted a canal to flood the ruins, and was later assassinated by his own sons, which was read as divine punishment for destroying Babylon. Esarhaddon rebuilt Babylon and positioned himself as its "governor" rather than its king. In 672 BCE he divided his two sons' roles: Shamashumukin took Babylon, and Ashurbanipal was made crown prince of Assyria. The arrangement was meant to prevent a repeat of the civil war that had attended his own accession. The episode says explicitly that this will come back later — because the brothers eventually turned on each other.

9:10 He got an education a king was not supposed to get
Ashurbanipal's education had already begun when he was made crown prince. He learned horsemanship, chariot driving, archery, military tactics and court etiquette — the standard royal package. But he also studied literature and history, knew multiple Sumerian and Akkadian dialects, and could read and write cuneiform. The episode stresses that kings of this era were not usually educated this academically, and often were not literate at all; literacy was the business of scholars and scribes. He was able to be this way most likely because early in life he was not being raised entirely as the heir to the throne.

13:14 In the reliefs, he wears writing tools at his belt
Ashurbanipal was a patron of the arts, building temples and palaces and commissioning vast numbers of reliefs. Many depict him fighting, lion hunting, and going about daily life amid wealth and luxury; some show the severed heads of enemies. The episode singles out one detail: in many depictions he wears a riding stylus at his belt, including in scenes where he is swinging a sword to kill a lion — Holly jokes that he probably wanted to write in his diary after killing the lion. The reliefs from his reign are considered the peak of Assyrian art, and the lion hunt reliefs are now in the British Museum.

15:19 Cruelty was not his invention; he took it to an extreme
The episode draws a clear distinction: practices like displaying enemies' severed heads were the norm among rulers in ancient Mesopotamia; but in his own commissioned depictions and in the records others left, Ashurbanipal is seen as having pushed this to an extreme. Specific examples include: salting the land after putting down a revolt, forcing people to grind up their ancestors' bones to make bricks for a palace, making the defeated Elamite king pull his chariot in the triumphal procession, and forcing one rival to live in a dog kennel. About that rival, some accounts say he was forced to wear a dog collar, others that a chain was run through his jaw.

21:39 This was the earliest "systematically collected" library
The library was built in the capital, Nineveh, and tablets have been found in the Southwest Palace, the North Palace, and around the temples of Ishtar and Nabu. The episode stresses two things: first, it is unclear whether these were the library's original storage locations or the result of tablets scattering after the city's destruction; second, this is one of the earliest known libraries to be systematically acquired and organized, a deliberately collected and curated body of knowledge, and the world's largest collection of Assyrian texts. Excavations yielded more than twenty thousand tablets and fragments, many bearing standardized colophons, indicating a systematic method of labeling and cataloguing. The total number of complete tablets is actually unknown.

22:39 He ordered the whole empire to hand over books, and knew who to ask
Ashurbanipal ordered temples and palaces across the empire to send texts to Nineveh, usually by having a copy made, with him receiving the copy or the original. Surviving documents show he actually wanted the originals, and that subordinates may have "creatively misinterpreted" the instructions in order to keep originals in their own temples or collections. Surviving correspondence also shows he knew exactly where to look for the texts he wanted, and who might hold works he did not know about but that were worth acquiring. Holly describes him as having a network of scholarly acquisition librarians. Some texts in the library were written by him, and many tablets carry colophons in his hand.

item.content:encoded:
Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born on the wettest grassland in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things up by ten or twenty years.

Diamond is 89, talking about leaders, geographic determinism, Papua New Guinea and Bach cantatas. Medium information density, but the back half — on environmental optimism and writing method — is where the value is.

1:09 No irreplaceable leaders, only irreplaceable timing
Diamond's answer to ‘who is the most irreplaceable leader in human history’ is ‘no one.’ Not because leaders don't matter, but because time washes out the difference: Jesus was a charismatic founder, but the Roman Empire of the same period had half a dozen other prophets; Genghis Khan built the largest land empire from China to Poland, but recent research found that the wettest period on the steppe in the past two thousand years fell right around his birth — had he been born twenty years earlier or two hundred miles farther away, we would never have known his name. From this Diamond distinguishes two kinds of questions: why you and I speak English right now has its answer in the domesticable plants and animals of the Fertile Crescent, nothing to do with individuals; why Amazon is what it is today has its answer in Bezos alone.

13:50 Rachel Carson moved environmentalism up by ten years
Cowen challenges Diamond with the environmental Kuznets curve: once per capita income hits 28,000, countries turn green on their own — is Carson replaceable? Diamond concedes the movement would have come anyway, but stresses she at least moved it up by about ten years — the day after her Silent Spring was published, a senator announced a government investigation into toxic chemicals. More crucial was her position at the time: in that era a professional scientist writing popular science was seen as ‘selling out,’ and she was not a university professor, so no one could say that of her; she was a woman, wrote like a poet, and would read her drafts aloud to hear them. Diamond says even today's best science writer, Richard Dawkins, doesn't write as well as she did.

18:00 The pomegranate juice industry waited five thousand years to appear
Cowen tests Diamond's substitutability theory with the pomegranate juice industry: without the Resnick family, America would eventually have gone down this road anyway. Diamond says no. Pomegranates were domesticated five or six thousand years ago, but there was never a global pomegranate juice industry, because pomegranate juice is extremely hard to make — you cut an orange and squeeze, but the pomegranate's value is inside an extremely hard rind, and the contents are not pulp but small seeds; scaling up requires a three-story-tall tower that crushes whole pomegranates rind and all. In 2002 America had 22 pomegranate growers, 21 of them small farmers with no money and no incentive. Lynda Resnick put in about two hundred million dollars and waited 18 years before starting to make money. Companies like Coca-Cola and Nestlé would never allow a division to invest 150 million dollars and lose money for 18 years.

29:32 Face-to-face social skill is falling off a cliff
Diamond's advice to a 25-year-old who wants to become influential: learn to talk to people face to face, put down indirect communication tools. He has done 60 years of fieldwork in Papua New Guinea and watched Chevron bring in international lawyers from Switzerland to negotiate with villagers who had never left their village — the lawyers thought they'd close it in a day, but the agreement reached on day one, on day two the villagers said ‘we've forgotten that agreement, the people who signed it don't count, these are a few other negotiators.’ The villagers had negotiated face to face their whole lives, with far more skill than the international lawyers. Diamond says over the past 40 to 50 years he has watched social skills degrade, and in his 39-year-old child's generation it is especially striking, because most communication is no longer face to face and people no longer understand each other.

33:54 New Guineans may be smarter than Westerners
Diamond answers ‘yes’ outright, and says some people hate him for it. His argument is that natural selection pushed in different directions: over the past ten thousand years European survival depended mainly on surviving smallpox, tuberculosis, measles and other infectious diseases, with little to do with intelligence; the main causes of death in New Guinea were coping with an extremely difficult environment and coping with other New Guineans — warfare there was constant. So his impression is that New Guineans on average ask more questions and are smarter. He adds that Westerners usually think they are stupid because they use stone tools — but they lack metal tools because agricultural output was far lower, not because of intelligence. Cowen presses him on a Nature paper claiming West Eurasians have gotten smarter since the Stone Age; Diamond says he hasn't seen it, but for more than a century eugenicists have been trying to prove Europeans are smarter, with no evidence at all.

39:24 The Industrial Revolution happened in Britain because it is an island
Diamond rejects Greg Clark's hypothesis that the British became more patient by intermarrying and lowering their time preference. His explanation is geography: Britain is an island, needs no standing army, and is not constantly invaded — the last successful invasion was 1066. Not needing an army, it gradually developed democracy, and democracy is a productive form of government. Britain also sits on the Atlantic coast, and like the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal, it was one of the countries able to spread across the world, because the Atlantic coast was the testing ground for seafaring technology. He notes that in the 1600s Britain cut off its king's head and Parliament became powerful. As for Daron Acemoglu and Jim Robinson's extractive vs. inclusive institutions theory, Diamond says he has learned more from Jim Robinson than from any individual in the past 20 years, but thinks they give geography less weight than he does.

44:32 Big business and young people have made him cautiously optimistic
Diamond says 20 years ago he would have said the most evil and destructive force in the world was big business, which at the time basically didn't care about the environment. But over the past 20 years big business has come to care more and more: Walmart leads on sustainable products, Unilever leads on sustainable fisheries, even oil companies. In 1999 the World Wildlife Fund sent him to do an environmental study of Chevron's oil field in Papua New Guinea, and he expected it to be terrible, but found Chevron extremely cautious, because they knew that if they screwed up, New Guineans would sue them and they wouldn't get the Norwegian oil field development contract either. Another source of optimism is young people: 25 years ago young people didn't care about the environment, now they care very much. The probability he gives is 51% good outcome, 49% bad.

47:46 The most important question is not to find the most important question
Cowen asks what the biggest environmental problem is at the global macro level, and Diamond laughs and says this is what makes interviewing Diamond frustrating: his answer is always ‘the most important thing is not to go looking for that one most important thing, because the world is complicated.’ He uses marriage as an analogy: a couple about to marry asks what the single most important thing for a happy marriage is, and the answer is not to go looking for that one most important thing — you need to get 37 things right, and if you get 36 right but disagree on sex or religion, the marriage breaks. Back to the question itself, he says there are three things we must get right: climate change, inequality, and nuclear risk — including the risk of nuclear war and nuclear winter.

item.title: AI Is a Rounding Error for Ordinary People: Diffusion Takes Fifty Years, Backlash Won't Wait
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
item.description: The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is coming too fast.
item.content:encoded:
The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is coming too fast.

An eight-minute short take, not especially dense, but it offers a counterintuitive angle: AI's biggest risk isn't technical failure, it's that ordinary people can't feel the benefits.

0:00 AI is still a rounding error in daily life
The author spent a few weeks on his honeymoon without touching AI at all, and on returning realised: the points where ordinary people encounter AI are either marginal or confusing. The positive impressions are making fun images and an enhanced Google search; the negative ones are addictive social media algorithms, a friend of a friend hooked on AI chatbots, and various claims about data centers. Family, food, transport, entertainment — the core of daily life — have barely changed directly. His conclusion: being obsessed with AI is the result of a very small number of people actively choosing it, and only by stepping outside the bubble do you see that what's happening today really isn't that important to most people.

0:00 The Industrial Revolution gave physical things; AI gives indirect benefits
The first Industrial Revolution brought cheaper clothes, cookware, reading material and new livelihoods; the second brought sewing machines, food preservation, indoor plumbing, photography, better light sources, bicycles and electrification — a long list, and a very physical one. The author worries that even if AI's benefits materialise (new scientific discoveries, treatments for rare diseases, sustained economic abundance), they are too indirect: ordinary people won't credit OpenAI or Anthropic with saving their life, because it was their family doctor who told them about the new treatment; and not many Americans will care that OpenAI solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem. He judges that fifty years from now, the daily life of the average American will still look a lot like today.

3:47 AI today is mainly a tool serving elites
Knowledge work is about half the US economy, and for that half AI is already (or soon will be) as foundational as electricity, with rapid agent improvements over the next eighteen months accelerating this. But a transformative, highly productive tool that only lifts half of society is highly unstable. The author cites the "Engels' pause": from 1790 to 1840 British workers' wages stagnated while GDP per capita grew rapidly amid technological upheaval. He argues that if the AI industry itself thinks this is the closest analogy, then backlash from those who don't benefit is reasonable. He also agrees with Doug O'Laughlin's judgment: knowledge-work output explodes while headcount in the tech industry very likely shrinks.

3:47 The backlash's root isn't AI, it's Big Tech's old debts
The author splits the political backlash facing AI into two layers: first, the early positive effects are too indirect; second, they are deeply intertwined with Western society's historical grievances against Big Tech. He stresses that the latter merely collided with AI in time — if AI's exponential growth had happened decades after the growing pains of platforms like Google and Meta, the data center issue very likely would never have risen to such a central political position. Solving either one would greatly relieve the pressure and give the industry more time to show positive reasons. And AI itself, through doom rhetoric and declarations of mass unemployment, has marked itself as a negative or unsafe technology, making both harder.

3:47 Robots might rescue the narrative for LLMs
The author raises an ironic possibility: if the intelligence explosion from mass-producing large language models spills over into robotics, accelerating robots' spread through daily life, humans will quickly seize on AI's tangible benefits. This is ironic because many people have been working hard to convince the public that this LLM wave is very different from the general AI progress of the past ten or twenty years. If in the end the same dynamic saves (or largely drowns out) the LLM narrative, that would be funny. He also cautions that robotics, autonomous driving and the current AI revolution are for now linked more at the level of storytelling.

3:47 Diffusion takes fifty years; the fight against it won't wait
The author calls the present the first five years of a fifty-year diffusion process, and lays out two simple problems: the positive effects are too indirect, and the political backlash is entangled with Big Tech's history. He judges that the story of diffusion will last far longer than the struggle against it. Young people paying attention today will, within their lifetimes, see powerful AI go from effectively 0% to over 90% full adoption. What truly marks AI's evolution is the kind deeply integrated into enterprises and acting as a personal assistant; it is only just becoming viable, and adoption will be far slower than for easily understood applications like ChatGPT. So continuing to push the technology forward is crucial — the benefits are astonishing but not a given, and there is still a great deal of hard work to do on distributing them widely.

item.title: Weather forecasts are 95% accurate, and nobody believes them
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-ologies-天气预报准确率-95-但没人相信它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-ologies-天气预报准确率-95-但没人相信它/
item.description: A meteorologist says forecasts are about 95% accurate in the three-to-five-day window, but the public only remembers the time it got rained on; climate is not future tense, it's present continuous.
item.content:encoded:
A meteorologist says forecasts are about 95% accurate in the three-to-five-day window, but the public only remembers the time it got rained on; climate is not future tense, it's present continuous.

Medium information density: the first half is career explainer, the second half — on probability, hurricane cones and climate lag — is worth your time.

14:27 The forecast isn't wrong; human memory is biased
The public broadly believes weather forecasts are often wrong, but the number Shepard gives is roughly 95% accuracy in the three-to-five-day window. The problem isn't the model, it's memory: people remember the cookout that got rained on, the kid's ballgame that got rained on, and forget all the days the forecast nailed it. He uses the kicker analogy — perfect all season, misses one in the Super Bowl, and that's the only one anyone remembers. What this changes: forecast reliability is far higher than its public reputation, and that reputation is shaped by statistical bias.

18:36 Bomb cyclone isn't a new word, it's new exposure
Many people assume bomb cyclone, polar vortex and derecho are signals that the climate has changed. Shepard rejects that outright: these terms have existed in meteorology for decades, they've just recently come into heavy use in mass media. So you can't use the popularity of a term as an anchor for climate change. What is actually changing is intensity — heavier downpours, more frequent and more severe heat waves, rapid hurricane intensification, higher sea levels pushing more water in with the same storm, bigger storm-surge losses.

22:42 The reason for optimism is that we know what to do
Shepard says he doesn't want to stop at bad news, because the good news is this isn't a problem that still needs head-scratching research — we know what to do: cut carbon emissions, and we must adapt, because some changes have already crossed irreversible points. He cites the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave: most homes there had no air conditioning, Canada recorded 120 degrees Fahrenheit, it was called a once-in-a-millennium event, but climate change made it 150 times more likely, causing nearly $9 billion in losses and 1,400 heat deaths. The adaptation strategy is to retrofit those houses with air conditioning.

28:06 Warming makes blizzards more intense, not less
The counterintuitive mechanism: hurricanes, downpours and blizzards all start with water vapor. The Clausius-Clapeyron equation says a warmer atmosphere holds more water vapor. For every 1 degree Fahrenheit of warming, water vapor increases about 4% (7% in Celsius). A century ago the Northeast US averaged 22 degrees Fahrenheit in winter; now it's up to 26, and some years 30 — that's a 32% increase in water vapor over 22, and 30 is still below the 32-degree freezing point. So a warmer planet means more water in the atmosphere, and blizzards can hit harder.

41:31 The hurricane cone is probability, not a path
During Hurricane Ian in 2022, some people evacuated from one part of the cone to another — a total misreading. The cone means the storm center has a 67% chance of falling somewhere inside it, not that the storm will travel down the center line of the cone. Shepard says the public broadly struggles with probability, uncertainty, two or more processes happening at once, and anything that can't be simplified to their level — so they simplify complex information down to their level, and the cost is bad decisions.

1:00:12 A 20% chance of rain does not mean it won't rain
Shepard tells the story of getting rained on while tubing with his son: the woman next to them complained that it was only a 20% chance of rain and meteorologists are always wrong. But that day wasn't 0% — they just happened to be in that 20% area. Statistically, 80% of the area stayed dry, and they landed in the 20% that got wet. One way to compute POP is confidence of rain × fraction of area affected: 60% confidence over 60% of an area gives a POP of 36%. So "20% chance" doesn't mean "it won't rain" — it's describing a regional probability distribution.

1:07:32 Satellites cover more ground, balloons resolve more detail
On the trade-off between weather balloons and satellites: satellites give more consistent observations over a wider area, while balloons only have data at the launch point and launch time, sometimes only twice a day. But satellite resolution is far coarser. Shepard uses a phone camera analogy: more pixels make a better photo, and the finer the resolution of an observation or model, the more fine-scale weather it can capture. A thermometer or barometer at your location has far better resolution than the blurry one-square-mile reading a satellite gives you.

item.title: Grok Bot shipped in a month: a small team hid in a cave, a big team would have micro-decisioned it to death
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-lennys-grok-bot-一个月做出来-小团队躲进山洞-大团队会拖没微决策/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-lennys-grok-bot-一个月做出来-小团队躲进山洞-大团队会拖没微决策/
item.description: Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, but users can smell three visions sharing one screen — that's shipping your org chart. So Grok Bot started from zero, a handful of people hid in a cave for a month.
item.content:encoded:
Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, but users can smell three visions sharing one screen — that's shipping your org chart. So Grok Bot started from zero, a handful of people hid in a cave for a month.

The first half is the trade-off detail of product decisions; the second half — that a bot should have its own computer, that automation shouldn't have a UI — is worth more.

0:02 Shipping a hit in a month came from a small team hiding in a cave
Grok Bot didn't start as a tab added to Cursor. It started as a team of "a handful of people" isolated in a corner of the office with a private Slack channel, going from first line of code to an internally usable prototype in about a month. Roman's judgment: with a big team and a 6-to-12-month vision plan, you wouldn't build the thing that actually shipped — because every day is a pile of non-obvious micro-decisions, and a big team drags those decisions to death.

9:07 Not putting it in Cursor: users can smell three visions on one screen
Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, and the team discussed it seriously. Roman says the problem with that path is "small paper cuts": the product feels oppressive to non-technical users, plus the brand association. He called out the competitor approach of "add a tab for every new form factor" — users can feel that this isn't one unified vision of work but three visions sharing one screen, like "shipping your org chart." So they decided to start completely from zero.

11:08 Two or three hundred manual onboardings, so tomorrow's mistake never happens again
The team onboarded two or three hundred people by hand, including the host. The first few were painful: the computer wouldn't start, the user was confused, and the core team had to sit on that 20-minute call. Roman says the effect of that presence is "that can never happen again" — fix it tomorrow, because tomorrow you onboard the next person. The pattern lasted about two weeks.

12:08 They deliberately didn't tell users what bots to build
Internally, a pattern emerged on its own: "5 to 10 bots each owning a piece." By the end of the second week, people started promoting a standout bot to primary personal assistant, then making it chief of staff and dispatching tasks to other bots — there was even a screenshot of a user telling a bot it got promoted, and the bot asking whether that came with a raise and a bigger token budget. The team noticed, but deliberately didn't guide it during onboarding, afraid of biasing users, wanting to see whether outside users would get there on their own. Many did.

14:09 Not showing the thinking process is a product stance, not laziness
Grok Bot hides a lot of internal machinery: no tool calls, no step-by-step of what it clicks on its own computer, just a Slack-like activity indicator and on-demand stage updates. Roman's analogy: you wouldn't ask a colleague to report second by second which button he pressed and which site he visited. Some feedback did ask for a to-do list and priorities, but nobody wanted long text streams and chain of thought — which confirmed the direction.

19:11 Those three weeks of internal beta were mostly unshipping
From internal beta to public launch was only about three weeks, and Roman says that stretch was "we unshipped a lot": cutting experimental features, moving pseudo-developer visibility tools off the product surface, like interfaces exposing the model's internal thinking and specific memories. The test was "what is the launch post" — if it can't be written as a convincing launch tweet, it probably shouldn't be built. He also distinguishes "Grok Bot now has" (new button, new dropdown, new integration) from "Grok Bot can now" (new capability); the latter is the right frame.

29:17 Automation shouldn't have a UI; 99% is generated from one sentence
Competitors' automation setup means going into a sidebar, clicking plus, picking a trigger event, picking an action. Roman calls that clunky, and the result is that people rarely actually build automations. Grok Bot's approach is to define it in natural language: tell the bot "remind me every morning at 8," and it should just do it — the user should never see the automation-creation UI. Today 99% of automations on the platform are built that way.

30:17 Two early decisions: everything in the cloud, every bot has its own computer
Roman credits Grok Bot's success to two decisions that weren't obvious at the time. First, users should never have to think about local versus cloud, whether the computer is on, or whether starting from your phone means connecting to the machine at home — all of it in the cloud, with the bot as a persistent colleague that has its own computer and is consistent across every entry point. Second, the bot must have its own computer, because a lot of tools have no decent MCP or API, and humans never worked through MCP and APIs anyway — they clicked pixels and typed into input boxes.

item.title: Picky Eating Isn't About the Food: Fix the Relationship First, Then Talk Nutrition
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-secureattach-孩子挑食别怪食物-先修关系-再谈营养/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-secureattach-孩子挑食别怪食物-先修关系-再谈营养/
item.description: The feeding strategy itself matters less than how you execute it; a parent's own relationship with food is the most effective intervention they can make for their child.
item.content:encoded:
The feeding strategy itself matters less than how you execute it; a parent's own relationship with food is the most effective intervention they can make for their child.

Medium information density, but the "health impact tiers" framework and the practical advice on "neutralizing food" offer direct relief to anxious parents.

5:05 The feeding anxiety starts at the nine-month checkup
Jennifer is a registered dietitian who did nontraditional work in the USDA's SNAP education program and considered herself someone who "knew how to feed a child." At the nine-month checkup the doctor said her child's weight wasn't keeping up, and she said that moment felt like the rug being pulled out from under her. For years afterward she worked to keep her child on the growth curve, and her second son showed early signs of extreme picky eating. Standing in the kitchen making lunch, she realized she couldn't be the only parent struggling this much, and in 2019 she started Kids Eat in Color, first posting feeding tips as a hobby.

12:12 The research behind "don't pressure your kid" isn't that strong
She says "don't force your child to eat" is a great slogan, and for some families that one line is enough. But after digging deep into the research on feeding pressure, she believes it isn't as strong as dietitians or feeding experts make it out to be, and parents actually have more room to experiment. The second part of her book deals specifically with "what to do if the standard approach doesn't work": first give the general advice, then give the alternatives that are considered less ideal but can be executed with reduced risk, which she calls risk reduction.

16:19 Put a small piece of green pepper on the plate five hundred times
The exposure method she teaches parents: put a small slice of green pepper on a plate full of foods the child loves. The goal isn't to get him to eat it, but to desensitize him to its presence. Maybe after five hundred times he sniffs it, then licks it, then throws it at his brother, then one day eats it. The precondition is that the child is in a regulated state — if the child hasn't been soothed, he simply can't try new things, because he's scared of something else. So first get the child calm before he sits down at the table.

23:22 An anxious child has a dry mouth and tight throat and physically can't eat
Sarah adds the neural mechanism: when anxious, the mouth goes dry, the throat tightens, and there may be nausea or stomach pain — these are exactly the signs of sympathetic (fight or flight) activation, while eating requires the parasympathetic rest and digest state. In other words, if every time you come to the table it's with dread and a power struggle, you are physiologically pushing the child in the opposite direction from eating. Play, jokes, and little games at the table work because they bring the child into that relaxed, connected parasympathetic state, and only then do saliva and swallowing come back.

28:26 A meal can be rescued from the worst possible start
She tells of one dinner at her own home: before the parents even got back to the table, the two kids were already fighting and one slammed the door and went to his room. They let that child calm down on his own in his room while the remaining three ate first. Fifteen or twenty minutes later the child came downstairs and started eating, the whole family was laughing together, and everyone was eating. She says the meal ended with the siblings fighting again, but the moment of connection in the middle was real. So don't hold yourself to perfectionism — there's usually at least one good moment in a meal, find it.

32:28 Sensational headlines can basically be swiped away
The first filter she gives parents: if the headline is sensational, you can almost conclude it's wrong, probably ninety percent of the content is taken out of context, so just keep scrolling and don't lose sleep over it. But if it's a real event — say an outbreak of diarrhea one summer, or a specific food recall — then pay attention. What she really wants to give is a tiered framework: the first tier is severe food allergies and insufficient calorie intake (ARFID, extreme picky eating, food insecurity), which can make a child seriously ill or worse and must be addressed first.

33:29 Protein and fiber are in the second and third tiers, food dyes in the fourth
The second tier is protein, and every meal and most snacks should include a real protein food. The third tier is fiber, because fiber trickles down: if a child eats enough high-fiber foods, he naturally eats less of the added sugar and added sodium. And food dyes, which grab the most headlines, are in the fourth tier, with a very narrow impact. She says that for the vast majority of children, artificial dyes won't change their health trajectory; for the small number of sensitive children, parents have most likely already figured it out on their own. Removing dyes from the food system wouldn't solve the childhood health crisis either.

43:35 Call it a "cookie," not an "occasional food"
To help parents who don't have a healthy relationship with food, her entry point is "talking about food with facts": call foods by their names directly — this is a cookie, this is a sandwich, this is your chicken, this is your sugar. Don't say "this is an occasional food, this is an everyday food," don't sort your child's food into healthy/unhealthy or good/bad, and avoid moralizing and black-and-white thinking. She says there's no evidence that black-and-white thinking directly causes eating disorders, but research has found that black-and-white thinking is very common in children with restrictive eating disorders, and hearing that "foods are good or bad" gets embedded in their restrictive thinking.

item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
