item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything their body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything their body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.

Most approaches restate "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that comes before the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and demonstrates the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 A child who hits is shouting that his body isn't his to decide
Preschool is often the first place a child is controlled in nearly every bodily arrangement by an adult other than a parent: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and when to move. For the previous three years he could roughly decide for himself when to run, when to use the toilet. Sitting on a rug for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body is mine to decide," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. So when the incident call comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself" — ask instead: how much say did this child have over his own life before this, and what small piece of it can be handed back now.

6:42 Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
Teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit still when the teacher says sit still, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. Parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. But what the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, need the children safe, need to save effort, and may even take satisfaction from the power; many went into education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over model of relationship. Seeing both sides' situations is what opens room to negotiate.

9:24 We grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children
If an adult at a party feels overloaded, he arrives early, leaves early, hides in a quiet room, even wears noise-canceling earplugs — we find that entirely natural. Turn the camera on a child, though, and apart from conventions like extra exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, he'll never survive the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back to the center of the loud party — swap in an adult and you instantly see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child we look right past it.

12:11 The repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself
Repeating "hitting is not okay" doesn't work, because that isn't knowledge the child is missing. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the few seconds before this bite? What happened earlier in the day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will melt down — so let him stand at the front, the back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. The adult analogy: when your partner snaps at you for no reason at night, it's usually not about that sentence but about the morning's argument, lost sleep, and a chain of stress. If the other person then tossed off "your attitude needs some work," you'd blow up too — yet we routinely do only the latter to children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, hear what the "no" is protecting
Telling a teacher "please change what you're doing" will almost certainly hit a wall. The safer opening is to drop judgment and reconstruct the facts: don't look for who's responsible, just ask what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you know whether the child's trigger is sensory or autonomy, extend empathy to the three things behind the teacher: competence, the children's safety, and the effort saved by catching a breath. The request must land on a concrete, executable change, like "can he sit on a ball outside the circle." If the teacher refuses, the keyword isn't the refusal but what need that "no" is still protecting, and finding a different approach that satisfies both sides.

16:07 A nap-time conflict, cleanly taken apart
Jen's daughter Carys, at three, couldn't nap, and the teacher wanted her lying down; she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state rules required offering nap time, and the nap period was the teacher's own rest time. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could quietly play with soft toys that wouldn't roll, and the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and her rest, and Jen escaped the no-win incident-call loop. This segment shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is held.

17:53 Every method comes down to one question
Compress all of the above into a single line: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting and kicking are only surface signals; the real message may be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meeting it can be designed — and it is almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

item.title: The Thai Flood That Wrecked the Hard Disk Drive Industry: The Biggest Factory Fell, the Number Two Took the Throne
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: the largest maker, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter over quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: the largest maker, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter over quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.

What are the risks of geographic concentration in a manufacturing supply chain? This flood is a complete case study — industrial estate siting, zero inventory and a single point of failure all detonating at once.

6:13 Flood walls gave the hard drive makers a false sense of security
The industrial estates were built on river floodplain converted from rice paddies north of Bangkok. To guard against flooding, developers installed ring levees up to two metres high, secondary wave walls, pumps and drainage systems; the parks quickly grew into small cities with their own housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season arrived in 2011, seven industrial parks were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that it was precisely this seemingly complete infrastructure that created a kind of false confidence — the belief that even if it rained, everything would be fine. In other words, what the manufacturers bought was not safety, but an illusion about risk.

8:24 Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
After the flood, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism focused on favouring farmers and rice-corruption allegations. But the research does not support that attribution. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios swapping the release strategies of two dams, and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could have been reduced by at most 3.68%. Another 2020 study examined hydrological station data along the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster zone, and reservoir decisions cannot carry the blame.

9:25 Why did Seagate, which was not flooded, also stop?
Seagate's factory in northern Korat was basically fine, but production still halted — because seven of its top ten suppliers were underwater. The typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives and shut down production outright after two plants flooded. The hard drive supply chain interlocks layer by layer: however safe the assembly line, if the motors do not arrive, the whole line stops. Seagate held its quarterly shipment decline to 8% by quickly qualifying new suppliers, modifying designs to reduce complexity, and negotiating payment terms with suppliers. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant took on water 1.8 metres deep, and its quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose underlying supply chain could route around the break faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced in March 2011 that it would acquire Hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later Seagate announced the acquisition of Samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. Precisely because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that fourth-quarter 2011 hard drive demand was about 180 million units, while actual production was only 110 million to 120 million; and the flood happened to hit the Christmas shopping season. Retail immediately raised spot prices by 20% to 40%, and a 1TB hard drive at Taipei's Guanghua Market went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion lower than expected because of the hard drive shortage. A local flood, transmitted through zero inventory, became a global shortage just like that.

15:41 The water receded, but hard drive prices did not fall for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive availability only returned to pre-disaster levels about nine months later; retail prices fell back even more slowly — hard drive prices on Newegg did not drop back to pre-disaster levels until April 2013. Backblaze did the arithmetic with its own purchasing records: in September 2011 the cost per GB was $0.044, and returning to that level again would take until September 2013. Why is it easy to raise prices and hard to cut them? The author lists several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the two giants' 2011 acquisitions brought extra costs, tablets caused PC hard drive demand to fall permanently, and a more cynical guess — after Seagate and Western Digital acquired their second-tier rivals, only three major makers remained in the whole industry, making prices easier to ‘stabilise’, or in his own word: cartelize. As for which one is the truth, he does not conclude.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and keep building walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat, it doubled down on defences. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometre flood wall along the estate, and WD added a six-metre-high inner wall around the factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reasons are not hard to understand: ready-made estates, supporting infrastructure and skilled workers are hard to pack up and take away. Thailand has since suffered several more rounds of major flooding, especially in the 2020s when it happened almost every year; in one recent November it even rained in what was billed as a ‘once in 300 years’ event, but these estates have held out so far. Whether stronger defences will be needed in the future can only be tested by the next big flood.

item.title: AI designs viruses that infect bacteria, but only 5% of the time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: For the first time, AI designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at only about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, AI designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at only about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests.

This episode takes apart the success rate of AI-made viruses, compensatory mutations and biosafety rhetoric, and also demonstrates how an observational vaccine study can be falsified by an E-value.

12:43 A vaccine switch as a natural control
The trap in "healthy vaccinee bias" is that vaccinated people tend to pay more attention to their own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the moment in 2017 when the US shingles vaccine switched wholesale from Zostavax to Shingrix: before the policy switch people received the old vaccine, after it they received the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. It is still not a randomised trial, however — unmeasured factors such as socioeconomic status, smoking and diet may still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it counts only as a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit
How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? Measure it with the E-value. The E-value for this vaccine study is only 1.42, almost hugging 1, meaning a confounder that is not even very strong but is associated with both "which vaccine was received" and "cardiovascular outcome" could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value needs to reach 3.4 or even 5 before a conclusion counts as solid; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves admit that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation cannot be treated as evidence.

38:13 AI produces a functional viral genome for the first time
The researchers took the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public DNA sequence data, then they were fine-tuned on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. Back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli — the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch that was then proven functional. If the media summarise this as "AI directly made a virus", they miss a key point: the model has only ever seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

44:37 The origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory
The only prompt the model needs is the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome, and the accuracy of the generated results rises significantly. The authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and that it was 100% conserved across all the genomes the model generated. It works like a password meaning "I am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be locked down, and only dares to let other positions evolve freely. This also explains why such a short prompt is effective — what matters is not the prompt's length but whether it hits a functional pressure point.

56:55 AI swaps one gene and adds 58 mutations itself
The design idea behind EVO36 was not to rewrite the whole thing but to swap genes: replace PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans performed the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the AI's EVO36 infects normally, because it accumulated an extra 58 mutations across the genome. These look like compensatory mutations that exist to re-adapt the foreign J protein to its local environment. Humans would not necessarily think to touch 58 positions at once, and this is exactly where generative models exceed the power of single-point editing.

1:00:15 Mixed phages specifically target resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 runs into a wall against already-resistant bacteria and cannot break through even after five passages; a mix of 16 AI-synthesised phages infected the originally resistant strain within one or two generations. Resistance is not broken by any single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining with one another during replication and accumulating new mutations, until the population as a whole breaks through the barrier. The result suggests that phage therapy should not bet on a single strain but should send in a cocktail of multiple synthetic phages.

1:07:29 Don't call AI-made viruses an urgent threat
For that study generating PhiX174, a contemporaneous commentary used the word "urgent" to describe its biosafety implications. Vincent objects to that wording directly on the show: the authors have already shown with reproducible experiments that this kind of research can be done safely, so what should be done is not to sound the alarm but to start building a safety framework. He also stresses that as long as you have enough sequence, reconstructing a virus is not science fiction — precisely why a framework is needed rather than fearmongering.

1:35:53 Not getting vaccinated is often just not knowing
Discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition, but because they simply do not know they should. Treating vaccine hesitancy uniformly as a "matter of belief" gets the policy response wrong — for this group the key is not debate or persuasion but information outreach, so that they first know the vaccine exists.

item.title: Sports Betting Has Infiltrated Gen Z, and the Regulatory Risk Is Underestimated
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/

item.description: Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy; slow losses are harder to recover from than one big blowup, and it sits on the same platform as financial products, with future regulatory risk widely underestimated.
item.content:encoded:
Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy; slow losses are harder to recover from than one big blowup, and it sits on the same platform as financial products, with future regulatory risk widely underestimated.

A multi-angle look at the hidden dangers of financialised gambling, from wealth management and market structure to regulation, with forward-looking value for understanding how the younger generation invests and where policy may change.

3:06 Gen Z treats betting as a financial strategy
A Betterment survey shows 26% of Gen Z investors see sports betting as part of their long-term financial strategy; in a CNBC survey, 52% of Gen Z investors moved money out of investments into sports betting over the past year. These numbers match Dave's experience with younger clients: betting has seeped into every layer of Gen Z and is now a problem wealth management has to face.

11:09 Slow losses are harder to recover from than a blowup
What makes sports betting insidious is that it rarely produces a dramatic blowup. Instead there is a steady drip of small losses — betting hundreds of baseball games over a summer, slowly losing 10% a week, occasionally winning 20% and feeling good, round and round. That kind of erosive financial despair is harder to recover from than one big mistake; it amounts to a chronic tax on numeracy.

17:14 Regulatory risk is widely underestimated
Dave argues most people ignore regulatory risk because they assume regulators respond to catastrophic events, when more likely some future administration or state regulator simply says "enough." He points to Florida and Texas banning speed cameras first, showing how unpredictable regulatory moves are. Companies depending on the current regulatory environment need to be on guard.

21:14 Leveraged ETF products raise market-structure worries
In the same week, South Korea set strict investor-education thresholds for 2x leveraged products, Japan explicitly rejected single-stock leverage, and the US saw a filing for a 2x leveraged product that resets hourly. What worries Dave more is that the new ETF tries to hedge gambling risk using the futures market, but that futures market doesn't exist until the ETF has assets — the order is reversed, and it could divert resources from important financial participants who stabilise oil prices.

25:20 Tech giants' earnings show "financial gimmicks"
Cameron points out that Nvidia extended receivables to help customers, while hyperscaler customers extended payables to flatter free cash flow; Microsoft reclassified some capex into investing cash flow, lowering its capex guidance; and activity inside SPVs doesn't show up in the statements. These "financial gimmicks" are common at cycle peaks — if the fundamentals were good, there would be no need for them.

29:24 Less disclosure worsens information asymmetry
Cameron opposes moving earnings reports to semi-annual and cutting disclosure, arguing it worsens information asymmetry, benefits institutions with the resources to assemble information through the "mosaic effect," and reduces market efficiency. He also notes that regulatory trends such as overturning the Chevron doctrine all concentrate power at the top, which is bad for innovation and competition.

38:27 The line between cultural appropriation and embrace
Cameron criticises Urban Outfitters for selling Nirvana tie-dye sweatpants to 12-year-olds, calling it a lack of respect for the context, but Dave argues it can be a gateway to the music: even a kid who starts out liking only the smiley face might end up listening to "Heart-Shaped Box." The argument reflects the tension between gatekeeping and openness in how culture spreads.

47:35 Finding adult role models means accepting imperfection
Dave shares a story about Keith Morris defusing a conflict at a Circle Jerks show, which sparks a discussion about role models. Cameron notes that as people age they learn to appreciate others' strengths while accepting their flaws, just as they do with their parents, taking the good and leaving the rest. Dave admits he can't find a living role model because he knows no one is perfect.

item.title: Ion Drives: The Slow Rockets That Win Space
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.description: Rockets aren't necessarily better the more powerful they are. An ion engine's thrust is as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet it can run continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny amount of propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics.
item.content:encoded:
Rockets aren't necessarily better the more powerful they are. An ion engine's thrust is as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet it can run continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny amount of propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics.

This episode covers ion propulsion's principles, limits and applications in full — suited to anyone who wants a systematic understanding of why electric propulsion is now mainstream for deep space and satellites; those with no taste for engine detail can focus on the thrust and applications segments.

1:04 Ion propulsion wins on endurance
The rocket equation is cruel: to go faster you must throw away more mass or throw it faster, but carrying more propellant makes the vehicle heavier, trapping you in a tax-collector's loop. Chemical rockets use high thrust to escape Earth quickly, but exhaust velocity is capped by the energy stored in chemical bonds. Ion propulsion takes another route: instead of burning fuel, it uses electric fields to accelerate a small number of charged particles to extremely high speeds and throw them out. The thrust is astonishingly small, but it can persist for weeks, months or even years, ultimately accumulating a velocity change chemical rockets struggle to match.

4:04 Specific impulse and thrust can't both be had
Specific impulse measures how efficiently propellant is used; chemical rockets manage only a few hundred seconds, while ion engines reach several thousand. But that efficiency rests on extremely low thrust: an ion engine can never lift off from the surface of Earth, the Moon or Mars — at most it can depart a small asteroid that an astronaut could jump off into space. It isn't physically impossible; it trades thrust for efficiency, and time for speed. Chemical rockets are sprinters, ion engines are marathoners.

6:07 Two mainstream forms of electric propulsion
The classic gridded ion thruster ionises propellant atoms and accelerates them out through charged grids — high efficiency, but the grids are continuously eroded. Hall thrusters use electromagnetic fields to ionise and accelerate propellant, with somewhat lower specific impulse but greater thrust, better suited to satellites, and they are the mainstay of modern electric propulsion. There are also micro electric propulsion systems for small satellites, and plasma concepts aimed at high power — the core difference among these approaches ultimately comes down to how to get enough electrical power.

10:13 Why xenon is the default propellant
Propellant choice isn't intuitive: at the same accelerating voltage, helium ions fly fastest and xenon slowest, but thrust depends on momentum — mass times velocity — so helium looks tempting. Yet at the same power, higher exhaust velocity actually means lower thrust; helium needs about 590 megajoules to ionise a kilogram, xenon only about 9 megajoules. Xenon is an inert gas that doesn't corrode the engine. It is today's high-end choice for ion propulsion, but costs about a thousand dollars per kilogram. Argon is far cheaper and is the industrial choice of the future.

18:20 Slow rockets are the bedrock of space logistics
Ion propulsion is especially suited to missions already in orbit: spiralling orbits up or down, rendezvousing with low-gravity small bodies. Humans are impatient cargo, but supplies — water, metal, parts, propellant — don't care about being shipped slowly. Future Mars plans or lunar bases can use chemical or nuclear thermal propulsion to move people fast, while ion engines deliver the cargo slowly ahead of time. Machines do the dull work; the history of civilisation is written in freighters, ships, railways, trucks and shipping containers.

26:25 Longevity is the core requirement, not a bonus
An ion thruster must run continuously for thousands or even tens of thousands of hours; grids erode, cathodes fail, power processing units must survive years of operation. A chemical engine burns for only minutes, an ion engine for years — this isn't easier, it's a different direction in which things get hard. It also struggles to exploit the Oberth effect: a chemical rocket can burn hard and briefly at orbital perigee for a huge gain in orbital energy, while an ion engine's thrust is spread over months and loses that advantage for nothing.

30:26 Propellant isn't fuel, it's money
Propellant isn't just fuel; it is mass that must be launched, mined, processed, stored, transferred and protected. Every kilogram of propellant saved is another kilogram of instruments, shielding, cargo and lifetime. The key to the early space age was whether you could reach space; the key to the next era is whether you can move around in space cheaply. Ion propulsion isn't enough to put people on Mars, but it may be the key tool for building space infrastructure — exploration gets the headlines, logistics builds civilisation.

31:26 Low-speed engines can build an interstellar civilisation
Today's ion engines cannot perform interstellar flight within a human lifetime, but far-future electric propulsion — with megavolt or even gigavolt accelerators, enormous power supplies and propellant measured in tonnes — would begin to approach an interstellar precursor vehicle. More importantly, even if ion engines never become interstellar engines, they remain key to building the infrastructure of an interstellar civilisation: before launching a starship you need to build collectors, mines, fuel depots, telescope arrays, habitats and shipyards. These must be moved, assembled, maintained and resupplied, and ion propulsion may be the best choice for that slow work. It isn't the starship engine itself; it is one of the engines that builds the civilisation that then builds the starship.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops: AI Can Reach the Peak, but Choosing the Next Mountain Still Takes a Human
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.description: Companies are being rebuilt as a series of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, picking the next mountain still depends on human intuition.
item.content:encoded:
Companies are being rebuilt as a series of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, picking the next mountain still depends on human intuition.

A structural judgment from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten by loops, and the biggest opportunity in consumer AI is joy, not efficiency. The takes are often counterintuitive — good for stress-testing your own product roadmap.

4:05 The AI era will not reproduce winner-take-all
The AI era will not play out the way mobile internet did, with winner-take-all dynamics: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, whereas every layer of the AI stack now has roughly 20 relevant participants. Two years ago everyone thought coding agents would end up with a single winner, yet today Claude Code, Codex, Lovable and Replit are all moving forward at once. Anish says the people at the frontier inside the labs believe what is actually happening is autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own processes — rather than recursive self-improvement, so there will be no runaway winner that swallows everyone. The takeaway for founders: don't bet on a single full-stack giant; every layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has a long-term place.

10:08 CEOs want to build bigger companies, not fewer employees
Employees probably don't need to worry too much about being replaced by AI — not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because a CEO's incentive is growth, not shrinking. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion company. A Google executive friend told Anish the company isn't laying people off but using AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and the hard problem has become ‘what should we add to the roadmap’. When execution is no longer scarce, attention shifts from saving labor to finding new things to do for a bigger goal.

15:12 Companies will become loops, and the next step needs a human to set it
The shape of a company is shifting from a list of roles and departments into a cascade of loops: first the automation of an individual's workflow, then functional loops, then loops that cross business units, until eventually loops run most of the company's operations. The loops themselves keep producing output, and that output becomes the input to the next layer of loops; some mechanism feeds the signal back to the CEO — when to adjust the business entity, when the strategy should change. This machinery can help a company climb to a local maximum, but after the plateau it must rely on human intuition to do out-of-distribution thinking and put the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Asking AI to directly come up with a million-dollar idea often fails, because humans can set the right direction while AI is only responsible for sweeping along a given slope.

32:24 Users want to spend time, not save it
Silicon Valley defaults to efficiency as AI's value, and Anish thinks that's a misjudgment: most people don't actually want to save time, they want to spend it where it brings connection, love, progress and fun. The biggest products in history have always been entertainment and social, so the consumer opportunity in AI is not ‘a few more minutes saved’ but building loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, and feel progress or fun. He criticizes the past 40 years of technology for extending intelligence while barely extending the soul; fitting AI into these desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

37:29 AI is decoupling skill from desire
Anish sees AI not just as a productivity tool but more like an emotional and spiritual interface — it can split ‘skill’ and ‘desire’ apart. People who want to make music are no longer blocked by ‘I can't play piano’; people who want to write code don't have to first learn it to the level of holding a job; personal identity is amplified as a result. He looks back at the high-risk environment of the 1950s-60s, which greatly stimulated human potential, and argues today's world is in a low-risk state; AI has a chance to pull GDP growth from 2% to 10-15% — provided it raises not the speed of a single link but the scale of what a group dares to imagine.

1:04:42 Ideas that are too small now fail to raise money
Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds would often say a $100 million seed round was absurd; today, looking at deals at a16z, the standard has flipped — if an idea can still only be that small with AI's help, they simply don't invest. ‘Unbounded ambition’ has become the core value for screening companies; Marc Andreessen's version is: we either go to the moon, or we leave a moon-sized crater.

1:09:48 Shipping something small every week is how you build product intuition
The most direct advice for product people is the old line: build more things. Find a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a ‘chassis’, run each new model through it, ship the finished thing, discuss it with people — that's the path to building AI intuition. The cadence only needs to be one small release a week; going crazy isn't sustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and the photo album, auto-scoring it, and finally generating 20 pages reviewing their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. It's small, but work like this lets you taste AI's ‘moments of joy’ over and over — once you've tasted it, you can't go back.

item.description: US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became targets that drew in conflict. The heavier they fought, the more bloated they became, losing mobility until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.
item.content:encoded:
US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became targets that drew in conflict. The heavier they fought, the more bloated they became, losing mobility until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.

Wesley Morgan lived the Afghan battlefield and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the War on Terror: tactical success coexisting with strategic failure, worth pondering for anyone watching war and organizations.

5:00 The outpost became a dangerous bubble
In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan entered Afghanistan's Pech Valley with the troops and found that US outposts meant to provide security for villages had in fact become ‘dangerous bubbles’ that drew conflict toward the villagers. US forces and the enemy rarely took casualties; it was the villages outside the outposts that truly suffered. This contrast made him start asking: who built these outposts, why, and when — questions that ultimately led to his book The Hardest Place.

10:39 The US military grew heavier and dumber
From 2006 to 2010, US forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, tethered to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006 the 10th Mountain Division could still reach remote areas by pickup and ATV, but by 2010, because of the IED threat and top-down force-protection requirements, conventional units could barely get to those places and had to rely on special forces for offensive missions. This overextension meant later units could not sustain the earlier reach.

12:51 Two ODA teams: restraint and recklessness
In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, used an ‘inkblot’ approach, trying to build secure zones around district centers and refusing to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something there was luring them in. The second, from Fort Bragg's 3rd Special Forces Group, was eager to get into the Korengal for a fight, got entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, was used as muscle for one faction, and started the Korengal ‘snowball’ that eventually became a fierce battlefield lasting years.

19:27 Three US tribes inside the military were incompatible
In eastern Afghanistan there were three ‘tribes’ within the US military: conventional forces; the Green Berets (working with local partners such as training Afghan National Army commandos and local police); and the Joint Special Operations Task Force (such as Task Force 373, made up mainly of SEAL Team 6 and Rangers, conducting night raids). The three had different objectives and sometimes supported each other, but more often got in each other's way. For example, the task force might kill someone conventional forces could easily have arrested, while only the task force could operate in remote areas conventional forces could not reach. This lack of coordination was a core problem of the Afghanistan war.

24:56 Commanders measured success with the wrong metrics
Many commanders lacked real understanding of counterinsurgency and could only rely on quantifiable performance metrics: ordnance dropped, miles of road built, number of meetings held. The book gives an example: 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, fought in Kunar Province for 15 months and lost 24 soldiers; its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent, and 10,000 Beanie Babies handed out — metrics that could not reflect actual effects and were even self-contradictory.

40:00 Navy admirals with ground-combat résumés
Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior US Navy and Air Force generals have a chapter in their résumés utterly unlike the conventional career path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Afghanistan's Kunar and Nuristan provinces — submarine officers, nuclear engineers, naval aviators. For example, current INDOPACOM commander Sam Paparo led the Nuristan PRT for a year. These assignments coincided with the fighting at Wana and Narisan, and they rode out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. That experience became a unique mark on their careers.

43:18 Military-media relations went from transparent to hostile
Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which unit to embed with, and public affairs just helped him reach company- and platoon-level units. But today, since the embed system ended in 2013-2014, military-media relations have deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of officers at battalion level and below sees the media as something terrifying. He argues the turning point was not the McChrystal affair but after Obama's second term, when the military began restricting embeds and pushing the war out of sight, because the complicated message that ‘advisors’ were really ‘combat advisors’ was unwelcome.

57:52 How Multicam became a mark of the elite
Morgan tells the story of Multicam's spread: it was invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art school graduate, lost the Army's camo competition (the Army chose the poorly performing ACU pattern), but Delta Force adopted Multicam privately because ACU performed badly at night. It then spread through special forces and became a mark of the elite. Crucially, Crye hinted to game producers that this was elite camo, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before real photos did, building an elite image in young soldiers' minds.

item.content:encoded:
In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on protesting students, killing 4. Confused orders, outdated tactics and an armed standoff turned a peaceful protest into a bloodbath.

This episode reconstructs the full course of the Kent State shootings, revealing the chaos and misjudgment behind the event, and it directly helps in understanding the social fractures in America in the 1960s and 70s.

1:05 The National Guard moves onto campus under arms
On May 3, 1970, 850 National Guardsmen carrying M1 rifles, bayonets and tear gas entered Kent State University, stationed at the football field and guarding the ROTC building. The deployment enraged students; even those who had not been involved in the protests felt the war had come to their doorstep. But students were not especially afraid, because previously the Guard had usually only used tear gas or gotten into brawls when handling demonstrations, and had never shot anyone dead. This time, however, what was unusual was that the troops carried live ammunition.

3:08 Orders were confused, and the governor poured fuel on the fire
Governor Rhodes's speech was full of inflammatory rhetoric, comparing the protesters to Nazi Brownshirts and the Ku Klux Klan and calling them "the worst people in America." But in fact, his order to formally deploy the Guard did not come until May 5, while the troops had already arrived on May 3. There were serious disagreements among the university president, local government and the governor over the Guard's mission: the president believed the assembly had been banned, but protest leaders and professors pointed out the ban had not yet taken effect. This confused transmission of information laid the groundwork for the later clash.

5:09 Rules changed on the fly, triggering a standoff
On the evening of May 3, students gathered in the plaza to protest, but local government abruptly moved the curfew from 1 a.m. to 9 p.m. and sent police to disperse them. Students saw this as "changing the rules midway," so they split into two groups: one went to the president's house to demand First Amendment rights and was driven back with tear gas; the other sat down on the main road, blocking traffic and singing "Give Peace a Chance." Police and the Guard surrounded them, with helicopters circling overhead. In the end, the Guard used tear gas and bayonets to drive the students back to their dormitories, leaving at least two students stabbed and 68 arrested.

9:11 May 4: a peaceful assembly forms again
At 11 a.m. on May 4, about 2,000 students gathered in the plaza again. Although there was no official state of emergency, university officials still handed out leaflets saying the assembly was illegal. Guard commander General Canterbury insisted the demonstration was illegal, but students still spread word of the gathering through loudspeakers. By noon the assembly was largely peaceful, with only some crude slogans. University police announced through loudspeakers that the assembly was illegal and demanded dispersal, but their voices were drowned out, and a few rocks flew at vehicles. Canterbury then ordered two rounds of tear gas, but they missed, and the wind blew the gas away instead.

12:13 13 seconds of fire, 67 bullets
The Guard advanced to clear the area and succeeded in dispersing most of the protesters, but one group of 52 pushed too far and was trapped in the fenced stadium, pelted with rocks. Ten minutes later they received orders to withdraw and moved toward Taylor Hall. When they reached the top of the hill, 72 Guardsmen turned, raised their weapons and fired a 13-second volley, 67 bullets in all. Four students died: Jeffrey Miller (20, 265 feet away), Allison Krause (19, 340 feet away), Sandra Scheuer (19, 390 feet away) and William Schroeder (19, 390 feet away). Another 9 were wounded, the nearest 60 feet away and the farthest 750 feet away.

14:16 One photograph changed America
After the shooting there was dead silence, and students stood frozen in place. Mary Ann Vecchio, 14, knelt beside Jeffrey Miller's body screaming, and John Filo, a 21-year-old photography student, took the picture that became an image that shook the nation. But the conflict did not end; protests spread across the country, followed by the Hard Hat riots, the Jackson State shootings and other events. The episode stresses that this history is strikingly similar to the present and worth reflecting on.
